name: Maryland Matters
title: The Prescription Drug Affordability Board is working, it’s time to press forward, not back
description: Despite what critics say, the Prescription Drug Affordability Board has not only made Maryland a leader in the fight for affordable drugs,  writes Vincent DeMarco, it will save millions for state and local governments -- and could save Marylanders tens of millions.
text:
Maryland's pioneering Prescription Drug Affordability Board has not only made Maryland a leader in the fight for affordable drugs,  writes Vincent DeMarco, it will save millions for state and local governments -- and could save Marylanders tens of millions. (Photo by Angela Breck/Maryland Matters)A recent op-ed highlighted the author’s personal story about struggling to find the right drugs to treat a health condition. Unfortunately, the op-ed also painted a wholly inaccurate picture of the impact of Maryland’s groundbreaking efforts to bring down the cost of prescription drugs.
The fact is that the state is on the right path to standing up to the big pharmaceutical corporations and making drugs more affordable for Marylanders who now struggle to pay for them.
A little background about drug costs is in order. 
Between 2008 and 2021, the median price charged by manufacturers for a new drug jumped from $2,115 to a staggering $180,007, and Americans pay roughly four times more than other wealthy nations for prescription drugs. These soaring costs cause increasing financial pain for many Americans, with KFF estimating that four in 10 Americans ration their medications due to cost. Drugs don’t work if people can’t afford them.
This crisis led to the creation in 2019 of the Maryland Prescription Drug Affordability Board, the first of its kind in the country. The board has worked diligently to set upper payment limits for certain high-cost drugs purchased by state and local governments. 




Your opinion matters
Maryland Matters welcomes guest commentary submissions at editor@marylandmatters.org.
We suggest a 750-word limit and reserve the right to edit or reject submissions. We do not accept columns that are endorsements of candidates, and no longer accept submissions from public officials, elected officials or political candidates.
Opinion pieces must be signed by at least one individual using their real name. We do not accept columns signed by an organization. Commentary writers must include a short bio and a photo for their bylines.
Views of writers are their own.




This year, the board established upper payment limits for the purchase of two drugs, Ozempic and Jardiance, by state and local government entities. These upper payment limits are expected to save state and local governments more than $6 million a year. Looking ahead, the board will have the authority to set upper payment limits for high-cost drugs paid for by private insurance plans effective Jan. 1, 2028, which could save Marylanders over $160 million per year. 
There is nothing radical about this approach. The federal government, thanks to former President Biden and Congress, has begun negotiating maximum fair prices on some high-cost drugs paid for by Medicare. After the government negotiated price limits on the first set of 10 drugs, prices for those medications went down between 38% and 79%, which is estimated to save Medicare recipients $1.5 billion in 2026, while saving the Medicare program roughly $6 billion a year. For the second round, the prices for 15 additional drugs are expected to decrease by between 38% and 85%, beginning next year. And it is clear that the Trump administration is effectively implementing this policy and will set negotiated prices on 15 additional drugs each year going forward. 
While the cost of these drugs purchased through Medicare are dropping significantly, there is no evidence that pharmacies are unable to stock and sell these medications – the central concern raised in the op-ed. Average Americans continue to get the drugs they need but at reduced costs.
Polling in Maryland and nationally show strong support for doing more to rein in drug costs. A 2025 poll, for example, showed that two-thirds of respondents nationwide support having Medicare negotiate prices for all drugs it purchases.
The General Assembly will consider legislation next year to give the board the authority to set drug upper payment limits for Marylanders that match the limits set by the federal Medicare program. This will create new savings for Marylanders as their health plans pay less for medications. Again, there is no reason to think this will lead to drug shortages in Maryland pharmacies.
Big Pharma continues to reap enormous profits at the expense of average Americans, while trying to confuse the public about the issue. According to a recent report by Public Citizen, the top 10 drug corporations in 2022 spent many billions more on advertising and profit-making activities than on research. It’s worth noting that the op-ed author is affiliated with the organization Color of Gastrointestinal Illnesses. This organization is directly funded by a dozen pharmaceutical corporations, as detailed in this Public Citizen report on astroturf advocacy organizations. We can expect the pharmaceutical industry to continue to create false narratives to derail the board’s work and preserve its enormous profits.
Maryland has been a leader in the effort to make drugs more affordable and now is not the time to turn back.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: These two midterm elections brought on new eras for politics in the United States
description: The conventional wisdom is that the Democratic Party has the advantage in the 2026 midterm elections and could become the majority party in one, or both, chambers of Congress. The margin of that anticipated victory is more difficult to predict. The size of a party’s majority makes a difference. To see why, it’s worth looking […]
text:
President Grover Cleveland (right) looks down during William McKinley’s presidential inauguration in 1897. Two years earlier, Cleveland’s political party suffered the biggest defeat in U.S. history during the 1894 midterms. (Photo from Library of Congress)The conventional wisdom is that the Democratic Party has the advantage in the 2026 midterm elections and could become the majority party in one, or both, chambers of Congress. The margin of that anticipated victory is more difficult to predict.
The size of a party’s majority makes a difference. To see why, it’s worth looking back to the second half of the 19th century, when two dramatic midterm election results marked the beginning of important eras in the nation’s history.
 
1874: A nation changing course
Most American college students, including the ones I taught for more than 40 years, learn that the era of Reconstruction following the Civil War came to an end when the contested presidential election of 1876 led to a deal that combined support for a Republican president with a commitment to withdraw federal troops from Southern states.
The Republican candidate in 1876, Rutherford B. Hayes, did not win the popular vote, but after an Electoral Commission established by Congress resolved disputed electoral college issues, Hayes won a one-vote victory. The White House had a Republican president, but the South was free to block enforcement of the post–Civil War constitutional amendments that protected the civil and voting rights of Black people.
That simple version of the story is not wrong, but it is incomplete. The 1874 midterms set things up for the controversies that would follow.
In the middle of his second presidential term, Republican Ulysses S. Grant was in trouble. There were scandals in Washington and economic hardships from a financial panic in 1873. The Democrats in 1874, amid accusations of fraud and voting irregularities in the South, won over 90 new seats in the House of Representatives and ended the era of Republican dominance on Capitol Hill that began with the election of Abraham Lincoln in 1860.
Before and after the 1874 midterm elections, white Southerners regained control of state governments and used violence and intimidation to suppress Black voter turnout.
Reconstruction was undone by a resurgent Democratic Party that after the 1874 midterms controlled both Southern states and the House. The compromise that removed federal troops from the South and put Hayes in the White House was icing on a cake that was baked in 1874.
 
1894: The Republican recovery
For two decades following the 1874 midterm elections, America’s two political parties were in constant and close competition for power.
Between the Grant administration and William McKinley’s election in 1896, no president won a majority of the popular vote. Between Grant and McKinley, no president had unified government — a single party in control of the House, the Senate and the White House — for more than two years. Not much got done.
McKinley’s 1896 election was the beginning of a new era of Republican Party dominance in national politics. It would last for decades, and McKinley’s successor, Teddy Roosevelt, would invent the modern presidency, with expanded executive powers and more direct communications with the American people. Political scientists call that kind of change a “realignment,” but it did not begin in 1896. Once again, the previous midterms made a difference.
In the fall of 1894, President Grover Cleveland, the former Democratic governor of New York, was in the middle of his second, nonconsecutive term. It was not going well. Another financial panic, bigger than the one in 1873, accompanied his second inauguration and set in motion a series of economic disasters that produced the largest economic downturn in American history before the Great Depression of the 1930s.
When voters went to the polls in the 1894 midterms, they gave the president’s political party the biggest defeat in U.S. history. Over 100 seats in the House were lost to Republican or third-party candidates. The realignment had begun.
 
A ‘wake-up call’ election
Huge seat shifts in midterm elections, like those in 1874 and 1894, are extremely rare. Smaller midterm shifts, which occur more often, can be a “wake-up call” that forces a sitting president to recalibrate political strategies.
That’s happened to many modern presidents: Harry Truman in 1946, Dwight Eisenhower in 1958, Lyndon Johnson in 1966, Gerald Ford in 1974, Bill Clinton in 1994, Barack Obama in 2010 and Donald Trump in 2018. Their midterm losses in the House involved 40 or more seats, losses large enough to put the president’s party on notice that something had to change.

Change came in different forms. Truman, Clinton and Obama fought back against a Congress with an opposition majority in the House and won reelection.
Eisenhower could not run again, and a weakened Johnson chose not to. Ford lost to Jimmy Carter; Trump lost to Joe Biden. All four turned the keys to the White House over to a successful candidate from the other political party.
 
What about 2026?
The 2026 midterm elections are unlikely to produce the kind of dramatic political changes that occurred in 1874 or 1894.
“Wake-up call” elections are much more common and more reasonable to expect. That result is more likely in a closely divided nation, with heavily gerrymandered congressional districts, because even a small shift in House seats matters.
Democrats don’t need a 40-seat swing to retake the House. If they flip a handful of districts, they become the majority party. In the betting markets, that appears to be the likely 2026 outcome.
Every president in the last 80 years who was underwater in presidential approval polling — as President Trump now is — lost seats in midterm elections. The smallest number of seats that flipped in those eight decades was five. A five-seat shift to Democrats in 2026 could make Hakeem Jeffries the Speaker of the House.
A 2026 midterm election in which Republicans hold their slim majority in the House would be a monumental achievement, even if it looked like nothing had changed. It would break a pattern that has been in place since Harry Truman was president in the 1940s and 1950s.
Most Americans pay more attention to presidential elections than they do to midterms. That might be a mistake.
A sizable midterm shift can signal large and long-lasting changes in American politics. A smaller shift can pull a president in a new direction or set the stage on which the next presidential campaign plays out.
The 2026 midterm elections will almost certainly produce significant consequences for American politics. The scale of those consequences and their longevity remain open questions that only American voters are able to answer.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa’s U.S. Senate candidates share fuel cost policies, trade criticisms on campaign trail
description: U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson and state Rep. Josh Turek both reiterated their calls for Congress to reduce fuel prices as they campaigned Friday for the state’s competitive U.S. Senate seat. At a news conference in Des Moines, Hinson reiterated her calls for the House to return to Washington, D.C., to work on lowering fuel prices […]
text:
Iowa Rep. Josh Turek, who is running for the U.S. Senate seat in 2026 against U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, held a roundtable discussion Sep. 25, 2026 in Des Moines about rising fuel costs. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson and state Rep. Josh Turek both reiterated their calls for Congress to reduce fuel prices as they campaigned Friday for the state’s competitive U.S. Senate seat.
At a news conference in Des Moines, Hinson reiterated her calls for the House to return to Washington, D.C., to work on lowering fuel prices and bringing the war in Iran to a close.
Hinson said she texted Speaker of the House Mike Johnson to “put the extra pressure on” bringing the House back to work. Johnson sent members of the House home Sept. 16 for extended district work. Hinson and other members of the House are not expected back in D.C. until after the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
“I think it was a mistake for them to cancel session,” Hinson said. “Every option should be on the table, and we should be in Washington, D.C., working to provide that relief right now.”
Hinson said Johnson responded to her text that “they are talking about it.”
Turek held a roundtable Friday with several Iowans who said the surge in fuel prices — due in large part to the ongoing war with Iran and closure of the Strait of Hormuz — are making it difficult for their businesses and families to stay afloat.
Hilary Abrahamson, a mother of four, said while she and her ex-husband are both making much more money than 10 years ago, she said “we had more freedom 10 years ago financially,” in light of recent high gas costs alongside other rising costs of living.
Abrahamson said the high gas costs were even more frustrating to her and many other Iowans because they did not believe the U.S. should be at war with Iran.
“It would be different to sacrifice some day-to-day things on behalf of a war people felt was necessary or benefited them,” Abrahamson said. “But from what I’ve heard, almost nobody feels they have any personal stake or interests, and it feels sort of like another pointless, forever war. And so, it’s really hard to sacrifice for something that seems totally personal to people you don’t know and have nothing to do with.”
Turek said while holding town halls and events throughout Iowa, “I have yet to encounter a single Iowan that said to me, ‘I want to be in another forever war.'”
 He criticized Hinson for voting against of a measure to restrict the president’s military powers in Iran — a war resolution that Hinson’s Iowa Republican colleagues Reps. Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks broke party lines to support. Four Republicans in the Senate similarly voted Thursday to require congressional approval for further involvement in the war.
Hinson voted with the rest of Republicans to block the measure in the House, which has been brought to a vote six times since the war began in February. Asked Friday if she would support the vote should the House return soon to D.C., Hinson declined to say yes or no.
“I like to take a look at every single piece of legislation before I (vote on) it, but I’ve made it very clear in my position: we don’t need another resolution on the House floor,” Hinson said. “We need a resolution to end the war as quickly as possible, and the president can do that.”
The Democratic candidate said Hinson’s vote was a continuation of “forever wars,” which some Republicans, including Trump, have called to end.
“In my lifetime, I’ve seen us spend a trillion dollars in Afghanistan, a trillion dollars in Iraq — for what?” Turek said. “And here we are again, another unnecessary war, spending over $40 billion dollars over there as we’re closing schools and roads and hospitals, leading the nation in farm foreclosures.”
In a social media post Monday, Hinson called for a “successful and immediate end” to the war in Iran which has contributed to hikes in gas and diesel prices. Iowa farmers have asked for immediate relief as they embark on harvesting crops.
Turek released a plan Sep. 16 to provide relief on fuel costs by pausing diesel exports, temporarily suspending the federal gas tax and opening the strategic oil reserves. He said this relief — alongside other policy positions he holds on tariffs, supporting rural healthcare access and improving water quality — are needed to help Iowans during a difficult period.
“Iowans are hurting and uniquely hurting — I think you can make the argument that we are hurting more than almost any other state,” Turek said. “I mean, we’re one of three states seeing our economy contract. You heard me give the numbers on where we’re at with health care. We’ve got a cancer crisis, we’ve got a water quality crisis, we’ve got public education that’s gone from the gold standard down to the bottom half. … And now, because of this war in Iran, you’ve got Iowans that are paying astronomical prices at the pump. Diesel price is at an all-time high and (so are) input prices. Iowans deserve to have someone in D.C. fighting for them.”
Hinson says ethics complaint is false
Hinson called a recently filed ethics complaint against her the actions of a “liberal group doing this for completely political purposes.”
The political action committee Defend the Vote announced Friday it had submitted an ethics complaint with the Office of Congressional Conduct alleging Hinson gave her husband, who works with the Independent Insurance Agents of Iowa, special access to her office and other congressional offices.
Defend The Vote Executive Director Brian Lemek said in a news release that Hinson should “know better” than to break ethics rules.
U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson held a news conference in Des Moines Sep. 25, 2026 calling for the U.S. House to return to Washington, D.C. to ote on a measure lowering fuel costs. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
“Iowa families struggling with rising prices deserve to know whether their congresswoman is working for them or for the insurance industry that supports her household’s business interests,” Lemek said in the release.
Hinson said the group’s complaint is a lie about her and her family.
“I have done everything ethically,” Hinson said. “I serve on the House Ethics Committee, and I look forward to seeing that complaint go exactly where it deserves to be, which is the trash.”
Turek criticized Hinson in a statement Friday, calling her a “corrupt, self-serving D.C. politician who has repeatedly shown that she is only looking out for herself, her donors, and special interests.”
“Hinson has sold out Iowans time and time again, voting to cut healthcare, food assistance, and Social Security – all while enriching herself and her billionaire friends and donors,” Turek said. “She voted seven times to continue this reckless war in Iran and Iowans are paying for it at the pump. This clear pattern of corruption is disqualifying, and it’s exactly why Iowans are going to reject Ashley Hinson in 39 days.”
Ernst calls for supporting Hinson in general election
U.S. Sen. Joni Ernst answered questions from Iowa Republican Party Chair Jeff Kaufmann at the GOP Reagan Dinner in West Des Moines Sep. 25, 2026, an event honoring her as she prepares to leave office. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Alongside the earlier news conference and a meeting with cancer activists, Hinson also spoke at the Republican Party of Iowa’s Reagan Dinner Friday evening, an event in West Des Moines honoring U.S. Sen. Joni Ernst. Ernst, the Republican whose seat Hinson hopes to fill, announced she would not seek reelection in September 2025 and went onto endorse Hinson in January.
Republican leaders including U.S. Sen. Chuck Grassley, state House Speaker Pat Grassley and state Senate Majority Leader Mike Klimesh gathered to thank Ernst for work in Washington, D.C., as well as her service as a state lawmaker and in the U.S. Army Reserve. When Hinson addressed the crowd, she reflected on her first meeting with Ernst over 10 years ago, when Hinson was a reporter for the TV station KCRG.
“Now I get to serve alongside of you and hopefully fill your combat boots, Joni,” Hinson said. “And serving in Washington, D.C., is true combat right now. And you have shown us the way, you’ve shown us the light, and you’ve shown us what it means to serve with dignity and purpose.”
She said defeating Turek in the November election is vital to preserve Ernst’s legacy and continue work on conservative goals. She claimed Turek was “masquerading as a moderate,” and said winning the election is needed to keep Democrats from gaining majority control in the U.S. Senate, saying Turek was aligned with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer.
“The reality is that this election on November 3rd will determine the balance of power in the United States Senate. It determines whether or not we’re going to have the wrong Chuck … making the decisions and calling the shots in the United States Senate,” Hinson said, referring to Schumer in contrast to Grassley.
Speaking with Iowa Republican Party Chair Jeff Kaufmann, Ernst also also reflected on her relationship with Hinson, saying she was happy to encourage Hinson’s first run for the U.S. House to unseat former Democratic U.S. Rep. Abby Finkenauer in 2020.
“I just knew we had to find the right person to run against Congresswoman Finkenauer, and Ashley was that person from the time I met her when she interviewed me all those years ago,” Ernst said.
Ernst said she felt more confident leaving the U.S. Senate with Hinson as the GOP nominee.
“When I went through that really tough decision, you know, whether to run or not — first and foremost, (I asked) can we keep the seat?” Ernst said. “It’s so important that Sen. Grassley have someone who will support those votes and vote with him and do the absolute best for Iowa. And it didn’t take me but a split second to to come to the realization that I know somebody who is absolutely ready to take that step and follow me in the United States Senate, and that’s why I’ve thrown my weight behind Ashley.”

name: Alabama Reflector
title: TikTok to pay Alabama $116 million in lawsuit settlement
description: The Alabama Attorney General’s Office and TikTok Friday reached a settlement over a state lawsuit that alleged the social media platform addicted children and lied about the safety of its platform. The settlement, coming about a month after the social media platform settled a similar lawsuit with the federal government, requires TikTok to install features […[...]
text:
In this 2020 photo illustration, the TikTok app is seen on an Apple iPhone. The company and Alabama settled a lawsuit on Friday that requires the company to prevent children from having access to its site in the evenings starting at midnight. (Photo Illustration by Drew Angerer/Getty Images)The Alabama Attorney General’s Office and TikTok Friday reached a settlement over a state lawsuit that alleged the social media platform addicted children and lied about the safety of its platform.
The settlement, coming about a month after the social media platform settled a similar lawsuit with the federal government, requires TikTok to install features that prevent teens from accessing the platform from midnight to 6 a.m. The agreement also requires TikTok to pay $116 million in restitution to the state and establish a $183 million fund for contingency payments, to be released depending on whether other states enter settlement agreements.
The consent decree, issued by Montgomery Circuit Judge Monet Gaines, also requires TikTok to provide educational resources to parents to protect their children while on the site and allows them to control the content their children view. It also requires the company to impose restrictions on minors’ access to inappropriate content.
TikTok did not admit wrongdoing in the settlement.
Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall said in a statement Friday it was a “great day” for Alabama parents and that they can “rest easier” because of protections that were established on the site.
“TikTok has agreed to give parents real control over what their kids see and how much time they spend on the app,” Marshall said in the release on Friday. “We’ve said from day one that our number one goal was to stand up for Alabamians when they are being harmed, and today, we did exactly that.”
TikTok said in a statement Friday that its priority “has always been fostering a safe and positive space where people can be creative, discover what they love, and connect with their community.”
“This builds on our commitment and core objective to continually enhance our robust safety tools to protect teens,” the statement said.
The Alabama Attorney General’s Office sued TikTok in April 2025, accusing it of “fueling a mental health crisis among Alabama’s youth.”
“TikTok’s so-called ‘safety features’ are a joke,” the office said in a statement. “They are nothing more than a marketing ploy to trick parents into trusting a product that TikTok knows full well is dangerous.”
The lawsuit accused TikTok of deploying an algorithm to keep children on the site to sell advertising, and accused the social media platform of harming their mental health, leading to self-harm and depression.
“The TikTok algorithm regularly exposes children to overtly mature and inappropriate content concerning alcohol, tobacco, drugs, sexual content, nudity, suicide, and eating disorders,” the lawsuit states. “This content, and the addictive properties of the app, are distinctly harmful to the still-developing minds of children and damaging to the State’s future.”
TikTok filed a motion to dismiss the lawsuit in June 2025, arguing among other matters the state’s claims were barred by Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act.
“Under Section 230, a defendant is immune from suit when: it is a provider of an interactive computer service; the plaintiff’s claims treat the defendant as the publisher of information; and that information is provided by another information content provider, not the defendant,” TikTok said in its motion.
The company also cited the federal Child Online Privacy Protection Act to challenge the claim made by the AG’s Office that the platform retains data from users. TikTok also said that the claims should be dismissed because the company was not  based in Alabama.
Friday’s settlement requires the social media platform to provide parents with resources allowing them to tailor the preferences and privacy settings and how to obtain information on their children’s accounts. It will also inform parents about how they view their children’s activity and their visibility on the site.
It also requires TikTok to create protections for teens to prevent interactions with “age-inappropriate accounts” and to provide age-appropriate content recommendations.
TikTok will also impose a ban for teen users during the late evenings to early morning by default. However, for those with permission to use the platform, TikTok will limit messages and disable some notification features.
The agreement also allows parents to impose limits on the amount of time their children may view the site. The default daily limit is set to two hours per day starting at midnight. The platform will also allow parents to see a summary of the children’s activity on TikTok and to schedule when they will be blocked from having access.
Of the $116 million TikTok will pay to Alabama, $14.2 million will go to attorneys’ fees and another $2 million will be for litigation. The remaining $100 million will be paid to the Alabama Attorney General’s Office for an unspecified purpose.
The company will also pay about $183 million that Alabama could receive in increments or tiers based on specific milestones. Tier one, for example, is worth about $55 million and could be paid out should the attorney generals’ offices from 10 states formalize qualifying agreements. Alabama is slated to receive another $55 million if another 10 states execute qualifying agreements.

name: Maryland Matters
title: State officials approve 14.6% rate increase for individual premiums on ACA marketplace
description: Marylanders who buy individual healthcare plans on the state's insurance marketplace will see a second year of double-digit increases to their premiums, after state insurance officials approved a 14.6% average premium rate increase across plans in 2027.
text:
Marylanders impacted by premium rate increases are urged to shop for plan options on the Maryland Health Connection. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)Marylanders who purchase individual health care plans on the state’s insurance marketplace will see a second year of double-digit increases to their monthly healthcare costs, after state insurance officials said Friday they have approved a 14.6% average premium rate increase across plans in 2027.
For the 274,000 Marylanders who purchase plans on the state’s insurance market under the Affordable Care Act, called the Maryland Health Connection, the new approved rate increases will compound on last year’s 13.4% rate hike that was issued in response to the expiration of federal tax credits that helped keep some plans more affordable.
Without those tax credits, more Marylanders struggle to afford their healthcare plans, leading some of them to downgrade their coverage or go without insurance, experts say, which further puts pressure on the healthcare system.
Insurance companies say the increased rates are needed to stay solvent and pay claims at a time when there is less federal funding to help offset rising healthcare and prescription drug costs.
Proposed rate hikes for long-term care plans would double premiums for thousands of seniors

“I think that the rates that were released today … reflect exactly what’s been brought Maryland’s way, following the expiration of the premium tax credits,” said Matthew F. Celentano, executive director of the League of Life & Health Insurers of Maryland.
He’s referring to the enhanced federal tax credits that expired in December 2025 after Congress failed to renew them. Celentano said the tax credits were “critical for consumers” and in helping keep healthcare costs down.
The 14.6% average rate increase approved by state insurance regulators on individual plans  is actually higher than the 13.7% average increase initially requested by health insurance companies in May and June. But over the summer, insurance companies amended their rate proposals asking for even higher rate increases.
State insurance officials say that the approved average rate increase of 14.6% is lower than what insurance companies ultimately asked for in their amended requests.
The approved rate increases announced Friday include an average 10.2% premium increase on small group plans purchased on the Maryland insurance market. Increases in the small group market plans were driven largely by increased inpatient hospital care and rising prescription drug costs.
Dental plans purchased on the insurance market will also see an 3% average premium increase, down from the 6.5% average increase requested by insurance companies.
Just how much the premium rate increases impact family budgets will vary based on several factors, including insurance carrier, plan type, household size and income.
For example, a household of four with an Optimum Choice Bronze plan may see a 3.5% rate increase, raising their monthly premium from from $975 to $1,009 a month, state insurance officials estimate, or a $34 per month increase. But a family of four with a CareFirst Bronze plan may see their monthly healthcare costs jump $302, with a 17.2% increase to their monthly premium.
Rate increases for individual plans bought on the Maryland insurance market will vary by plan. Here are some examples of what rates may look like for a family of four on a Bronze plan. (Chart courtesy the Maryland Insurance Administration)
The Maryland Insurance Administration notes that those examples do not take into account any subsidies that could lower monthly premiums for qualifying households.
But rising costs in healthcare and other industries are straining Maryland household budgets, leaving them to make hard decisions of moving to a lower coverage plan or dropping their plans altogether.
Maryland insurance regulators say that enrollment on the Maryland Health Connection dropped from 294,000 last year to 274,000 this year.
The drop in enrollment is expected to continue into next plan year – an additional reason why insurance companies asked for another year of steep rate increases, according to Maryland insurance regulators.
Vincent DeMarco, president of the Maryland Health Care for All coalition warns that the current state efforts are not enough to keep up with rising premiums and healthcare costs.
“We are disappointed that Marylanders will pay higher insurance premiums because of bad decisions by the Trump Administration and Congress, especially their failure to extend critically needed health care tax credits and cuts they made in eligibility. This is exacerbated by rising hospitalization and pharmaceutical costs,” DeMarco said in a written statement.
“Maryland cannot continue to protect our people without additional state revenue for health care and action to rein in skyrocketing drug costs,” his statement said.
Insurance Commissioner Marie Grant urges Marylanders affected by the rate increases to explore plans offered on the state’s Affordable Care Act marketplace. Those with household incomes that fall below 400% of the federal poverty level can qualify for state subsidies that may keep costs lower.
Grant also warns Marylanders to be wary of unauthorized health insurance plans in their search for more affordable insurance coverage.
“People need to shop and understand their options,” Grant said. “That (14.6% increase) may not be the rate you see – depending on your age, your family structure, your plan.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Spanberger proposes slate of data center regulations, puts first directives in motion
description: Virgnia Gov. Abigail Spanberger last week unveiled a package aimed at reining in the data center industry in the commonwealth, calling for tighter environmental regulations and for the industry to pick up more of the energy costs, among other proposals.
text:
Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger signed Executive Order 22 on Sept. 18 to kick off her data center regulation package. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)Virgnia Gov. Abigail Spanberger last week unveiled a package of legislative proposals to rein in the data center industry in the commonwealth, with goals to tighten environmental regulations, increase cost allocation for the industry and make the proposal process more transparent by barring non-disclosure agreements between localities and data center developers.
The plan does not include a moratorium on data center development while the details of the plan are refined, a step several environmental and advocacy groups and citizens have demanded in recent weeks.
Dubbed the “Data Center Accountability Framework,” Spanberger’s plan outlines five pillars as key priorities: transparency, environmental protections, lowering energy costs, promoting clean energy and focusing on local workers.
“The framework is a thorough plan to end data center secrecy, protect our environment, lower energy costs for families, bolster our clean energy economy and make sure Virginia workers have the protections and assurances they deserve,” Spanberger said as she announced the plan at the Virginia State Capitol.
Spanberger also signed Executive Order 22, which will kick-start her plans for clamping down on the industry ahead of the legislative session that begins in January.
Transparency
Perhaps the most concrete of the directives is a measure to ban nondisclosure agreements between data centers and executive branch agencies, departments, state boards and commissions. It also bars those agencies from requiring such agreements for data center projects.
New data centers in Maryland to get additional scrutiny under governor’s order

The order does not impact the use of nondisclosure agreements by localities, but the governor said she plans to work with the General Assembly to pass a law banning the agreements at the local level.
Spanberger’s package also proposes eliminating by-right local approvals of data centers that use more than 25 megawatts of power.
Many counties have taken steps toward requiring conditional-use permits, which require public hearings and a vote of approval from local leaders.
Additionally, the governor wants to remove data centers from Virginia’s fast-track permitting process on permits for projects in “business ready” locations. The fast-track process is a remnant of Gov. Glenn Youngkin’s administration, which encouraged and supported rapid build-out of the state’s data center industry to boost Virginia’s business reputation.
Environmental protections
The framework directs lawmakers to develop policies to create data center standards for energy efficiency, water use and land impacts.
Budget language that passed the General Assembly in June directed the Department of Environmental Quality to identify “water scarcity areas” where data centers’ water use for cooling could put drinking water availability at risk. Data centers in those areas, mainly east of Interstate-95, will have to reduce their water use.
The framework also outlines a plan to expedite noise regulations included in the budget language, but does not set a deadline for them to be in place. Currently, DEQ has until 2029 to research the lowest possible sound levels data centers could operate on and make that the standard across the board.
Lower energy costs
Spanberger’s framwork requires utilities to make data centers pick up more of the energy infrastructure costs incurred by the industry.
Dominion Energy has already taken action on that front, creating a new GS5 rate class that mostly includes data centers and large manufacturers. The State Corporation Commission approved the new rate class last November.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Like the recommendations in Spanberger’s framework, the new rate class includes 14-year contracts and specific cost allocations for energy generation, distribution and transmission.
The SCC also recently directed Dominion to create a new tariff to directly assign the cost of high-voltage transmission lines that are only necessary due to data centers to those customers. Spanberger supported the tariff, which is reflected in her framework.
Tech giant Microsoft has already put the State Supreme Court on notice that it could appeal that order. Microsoft representatives said in an email this month that the company hopes “any rates ultimately put in place are transparent, fair, and reflect the costs each customer creates.”
By filing notice of appeal, they continued, “Microsoft preserves its ability to challenge any implementation that does not meet these expectations.”
Elevating clean energy, hiring Virginia workers
Spanberger’s plan would also limit the amount of power data centers can produce on-site through natural gas generators and other “behind the meter” methods that don’t draw from the electric grid. But it would make it easier for data centers to bring clean energy options on-site, by reforming utility charges for clean-energy investments.
PJM, the regional grid operator for 13 states, including Maryland and Virginia, recently proposed a new rule to direct data centers to pay for their power generation or cover their energy needs by backstop power purchases. This would help bring more power on the grid when it’s strained on very hot and cold days.
Several recent proposals by data centers in the commonwealth show the industry’s growing interest in building its own gas turbines to power data facilities. That method skirts the Virginia Clean Economy Act, which requires utility companies to retire carbon-emitting power sources by 2050.
The framework prioritizes hiring local workers to build data centers and using local businesses for procurement and contractors.
Lawmakers, environmental groups, data centers react
Several lawmakers and environmental groups spoke up in support of Spanberger’s framework.
Counties scramble to respond to data centers, setting moratoriums, a ban

“Governor Spanberger’s Data Center Accountability Framework is a step in the right direction,” said a statement from the Virginia House Democratic Caucus. “We look forward to continuing to work with Governor Spanberger in the upcoming 2027 legislative session to develop thoughtful legislation that holds data centers accountable.”
Many of these policies would require legislative approval, and many are prospective, meaning they will apply to new data center applications but not the more than 600 centers already operating or being built statewide.
“For those that are up and running and already operating, we have the ability and intention to continue to make sure that into the future we are holding them to greater and greater standards,” Spanberger said.
Representatives from the Chesapeake Bay Foundation, Sierra Club, and League of Conservation Voters joined Spanberger for the announcement, calling it a strong first step toward legislation to cement the framework’s goals.
Other organizations criticized the framework for not including an outright pause on data center development.
“It does not address the continued connection of data centers to the grid, despite inadequate power and the many impacts on air quality, water supply, electric bills, and people and communities,” the Piedmont Environmental Council said in a statement. “Not to mention the hundreds of miles of proposed transmission lines, solely to support data centers.”
“We must stop the madness and issue an immediate pause on approvals until these protections – and more – are fully implemented,” said Chesapeake Climate Action Network Director Victoria Higgins.
The Data Center Coalition, the leading national group that lobbies for the industry, said it is waiting for more details on the plan.
“(We) are ready to engage with policymakers to ensure workable, balanced policies that keep Virginia competitive and honor prior commitments by the Commonwealth and its localities,” coalition representative Nicole Riley said.
Spanberger did not answer directly when asked why she did not impose a data center development moratorium while lawmakers consider her framework, but reiterated that some localities are considering pausing data center development.
“While [localities are] looking at what’s available to them as a potential option, it is up to our communities … But the state has to show leadership,” Spanberger said. “We are in a place where day by day, community members are demanding action.”
The framework, she added, “is an opportunity for us to take action and ensure that we are moving forward.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Hinson highlights support for bills to support rural cancer treatment, research in rural Iowa
description: U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson highlighted her support for measures to detect cancer and increase clinical trials in the U.S. House while speaking with advocates Friday, saying she would continue this work if elected to the Senate in 2026. Hinson met with volunteers with the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network (ACS CAN) as part of […]
text:
U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, who is running for Iowa's U.S. Senate seat in 2026, met with advocates with the American Cancer Society - Cancer Action Network at the Urbandale Public Library Sep. 25, 2026. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson highlighted her support for measures to detect cancer and increase clinical trials in the U.S. House while speaking with advocates Friday, saying she would continue this work if elected to the Senate in 2026.
Hinson met with volunteers with the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network (ACS CAN) as part of the organization’s “coffee cancer chat” series, nonpartisan events to discuss cancer with Iowa candidates ahead of the midterms. Many other candidates, including Hinson’s general election opponent, Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek, have met with ACS-CAN advocates in recent months to discuss their plans to address cancer in the state.
Cancer has been a defining issue in the 2026 Iowa election cycle because the state has the nation’s fastest-rising cancer rate, as well as the second-highest number of new incidents of cancer.
After cancer patients, survivors and family members shared their stories with Hinson about battling cancer, Hinson shared her own family experience of having her grandmother and two aunts who died of cancer. When she was thanked for sharing her own family’s experience with cancer, Hinson said “unfortunately, it seems like everybody has one,” saying, “that’s why we’re here and that’s why we do what we do.”
Some of the work on cancer treatment, prevention and research is already underway in Congress. ACS-CAN advocates thanked Hinson for cosponsoring the Clinical Trial Modernization Act.
Lori Johnson, one of the advocates at the meeting who was diagnosed with cancer in 2025, said the measure was “one of our big asks as ACS-CAN at the national level.”
She thanked Hinson for having staff meet with advocates about the bipartisan proposal that would  create a grant program supporting outreach, education and recruitment efforts for medical clinical trials specifically for underrepresented populations — including people in rural areas.
Hinson said the bill “really clarifies the gray area in making sure people feel like they can participate” in clinical studies.
Access to clinical trials is not the only issue facing Iowa’s rural healthcare system. Several rural hospitals have closed in recent years, and Democrats say the 2025 One Big, Beautiful Bill Act — the large tax and spending bill supported by Hinson and other Republicans in Congress which included Medicaid cuts — has worsened financial struggles for struggling healthcare systems and hospitals in the state.
But Republicans have argued the infusion of money from the federal Rural Health Transformation Program, authorized through the OBBB, will help rural healthcare providers in Iowa. The state was awarded $209 million in December 2025 through the program, which is set to allocate a total of $50 million to states between 2026 and 2030 in order to offset an expected  $137 billion decline in rural Medicaid spending over the next decade.
Hinson said the Rural Health Transformation Program ensures money is going to facilities most in need.
“You talk about targeting those resources directly to rural counties in rural America to keep those facilities open (so) they can continue to provide cancer care where people are — I think is really really critical,” Hinson said. “So that was a funding stream that I was very proud to support.”
Hinson also said she would also support increasing pediatric cancer research funding, pointing to legislation she introduced in August to provide funding for pediatric and rare forms of cancer through a “a portion of federal funds collected on imported tobacco products,” according to a news release. This measure, Hinson said, mirrors the 2025 state law signed by Gov. Kim Reynolds in May creating a tax on nicotine products like vapes and pouches with the first $3 million in generated revenue going to research, clinical therapy trials and leadership at the University of Iowa children’s hospital.
Hinson’s federal proposal would create “a dedicated funding path” for this research, she said.
“If this was able to pass, (it would) take some of the tobacco import tax money basically, and put it toward cancer treatment and research,” Hinson said. “So, if it had passed, it’d be $24 million just this year. So, it’s a little, but hopefully a little can turn into more. But, specifically for rare cancers and for pediatric cancers — and so those are two places that are traditionally underfunded or under-resourced as well.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Democrats, unions, advocates push for support on Question 3 on redistricting
description: Democratic lawmakers, labor union officials and nonprofit leaders rallied in Baltimore Friday to drum up support for ballot Question 3, the proposed constitutional amendment that would remove state standards for drawing congressional districts.
text:
Sen. Clarence Lam (D-Anne Arundel and Howard), backed by supporters of Question 3, speaks in support of the measure Friday during an event at the War Memoria Plaza in Baltimore. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)Democratic lawmakers, labor union officials and nonprofit leaders rallied in Baltimore on Friday to drum up support for ballot Question 3, the proposed constitutional amendment that would remove state standards for drawing congressional districts.
The event came the same week that supporters and opponents of the measure released competing polls that showed mixed support for it. Backers at Friday’s event said it is time to step up and start fighting for Question 3.
“We cannot stand on stage, wring our hands and express polite outrage at what [Republican President] Donald Trump is doing to this country, while refusing to use every single tool that we have to stop him,” said Sen. Clarence Lam (D-Howard and Anne Arundel. “Marylanders didn’t send us to Annapolis to sit on our hands, and our constituents expect us to act.”
Lam joined several state and local elected officials and representatives of a coalition of labor unions, nonprofit organizations and advocates from around the state at War Memorial Plaza in Baltimore to rally support for Question 3.




Ballot Question 3
FOR the purpose of clarifying that certain requirements apply only to districts for the election of members of the Senate of Maryland and the House of Delegates; authorizing the General Assembly to grant original jurisdiction to the Supreme Court of Maryland to review the congressional districting plan of the State; and providing that nothing in the Maryland Constitution provides applicable criteria for the boundaries of a congressional districting plan.




The rally came one day after Fight Back Maryland, a group working to pass Question 3, released a poll that said when voters were read the question as it appears on the ballot, 40% supported it, 35% said they opposed it and 25% were undecided.
But many told the pollsters that they just didn’t understand the question as written. When same voters were provided with a “positive messaging statement” about the question and then had it read to them, undecideds dropped to 11% and support rose to 53%, according to the poll.
That poll came just two days after Protect Maryland Votes, a group that opposes the change, released their own poll showing much less support for Question 3. According to the earlier poll, 41% of voters opposed the measure, 28% supported it and 31% were undecided.
Both polls surveyed 600 likely Maryland voters over several days in mid-September, and both had a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points.
If approved by voters in November, Question 3 would amend the Maryland Constitution to change the rules applying to the drawing of congressional districts and make it easier for the party in control to draw a map that favors it. Currently, seven of Maryland’s eight congressional districts are held by Democrats, with eight-term Rep. Andy Harris (R-1st) representing the Eastern Shore-centered First District.
Speakers Friday said the ballot question was a response to Trump’s push to get Republican-led states to redistrict to gain advantage in the upcoming midterm election, when the party in power typically loses seats in Congress. They also said it was a response to Trump himself, who they said has flooded U.S. streets with immigration agents — leading to the deaths of protesters and immigrants who were stopped — laid off thousands of federal workers and pushed gerrymandered congressional districts to decrease Black representation on Capitol Hill.
“For the first time since 1965, we are going backwards,” said former state Del. Vanessa Atterbeary, the Democratic nominee for Howard County executive.
“President Trump and his MAGA Supreme Court justices have repealed the protections outlined to us in the Voting Rights Act,” she said. “They have effectively eliminated any guarantee of due process or privacy rights, and it’s time for us to fight back.”
Part of that fight occurred in August, when the legislature convened for a two-day special session and passed the constitutional amendment that would become Question 3. The bill was struck down in separate court challenges by circuit court judges in Anne Arundel and Dorchester counties, only to be upheld on appeal by the Supreme Court of Maryland.
Former state Del. Vanessa Atterbeary, the Democratic nominee for Howard County executive, speaks in support of Question 3 at a Friday rally. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
The state’s highest court noted that the original question passed by the legislature was “misleading and therefore violates due process requirements.” Instead of striking the question, however, the court’s majority opted to rewrite the question and let it go to voters. That version is what voters will see on the ballot.
Even with the state Supreme Court State rewriting the question, Senate Minority Leader Stephen Hershey Jr. (R-Upper Shore) said in a text message Friday it remains confusing to voters.
“Gov. Moore and Democrats are now working overtime to turn Question 3 into a rallying cry in an election that has generated little enthusiasm or urgency among voters,” Hershey said. “It is apparent they need this question on the ballot as much to energize their base and drive turnout as they do to change congressional redistricting. Marylanders should be asking why changing our Constitution has become part of a political strategy.”
Sen. Shelly Hettleman (D-Baltimore County), who spoke at Friday’s news conference, acknowledged afterward that a friend had been confused by the question. After they talked about it, Hettleman said her friend, who doesn’t support Trump, understood the issue and supports Question 3.
“You’ve got to take seriously your right to vote and understand what you’re voting for,” Hettleman said. “That’s why part of what our jobs is to educate people about what is on the ballot, and hopefully they listen to friends and they listen to media that’s providing accurate information, and they go in as knowledgeable voters, and they’ll support it.”
For voters who want to cast a ballot in person, early voting begins Oct. 22 through Oct. 29. Election Day is Nov. 3.

title: Community members protest ICE after Bismarck-area detainments increase
description: About 75 people protested in Bismarck Friday to voice their opposition to immigration enforcement operations being conducted in the area. Sonja Mahlum of Bismarck said U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is “out of control.” “They are not going after the worst of the worst,” Mahlum said during the rally in front of the William L. […]
text:
Marian Krushe of Bismarck waves to cars passing by a protest on Sept. 25, 2026, in front of the William L. Guy Federal Building in Bismarck after immigration enforcement operations were conducted in the area. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)About 75 people protested in Bismarck Friday to voice their opposition to immigration enforcement operations being conducted in the area.
Sonja Mahlum of Bismarck said U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is “out of control.”
“They are not going after the worst of the worst,” Mahlum said during the rally in front of the William L. Guy Federal Building. 
The demonstration was largely in response to an increase in ICE activity in the Bismarck area this week, including two arrests that prompted a popular Mexican restaurant to temporarily close.
Rachel Patrie of Bismarck, center, holds a protest sign in front of the William L. Guy Federal Building in Bismarck on Sept. 25, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
The owner of Charras and Tequila posted on Facebook Wednesday that two employees were detained by ICE. They have documentation authorizing them to work in the U.S., according to the social media post by the owner, who was not identified by name.
“We work hard to run our business the right way, follow the rules, and provide jobs to our community,” he wrote. “These are people with families, responsibilities, and lives here, and I am deeply worried about them and their loved ones.”
A North Dakota Monitor review of the Burleigh-Morton Detention Center roster on Friday afternoon showed 19 people in custody who were arrested by ICE this week. The Bismarck Tribune, which began tracking ICE detainees earlier in the week, reported more than two dozen ICE detainees in the jail this week.
The restaurant planned to close for a few days, and remained closed Friday.
“Many of our employees are scared to come to work, even though they are legally here,” the owner posted. 
The owner declined an interview request on Friday. St. Paul attorney Nico Ratkowski, who is representing the restaurant employees, also declined to comment Friday.
Venezuelan men shipped to brutal prison under Alien Enemies Act ask court for due process

A spokesperson for ICE said Friday the two employees entered the U.S. illegally and have no legal status to remain in the country. The spokesperson said they will remain in ICE custody pending immigration proceedings.
“To be clear: work authorization or a pending application does NOT confer legal status in the United States,” the spokesperson wrote in an email. 
The Burleigh County Sheriff’s Office was notified that immigration enforcement operations were going to be conducted, Sheriff Kelly Leben said. 
“It’s my understanding that these are targeted enforcement operations and they have intelligence on what they are looking for,” he said. “To me, this would be what I would consider routine enforcement.”
The sheriff’s office monitored and assisted because of the tension across the U.S. with immigration enforcement, Leben said.
“We played a very limited role in the operation,” Leben said.
Nick Chase, U.S. attorney for North Dakota, said Friday his office has not charged any criminal cases in connection with ICE arrests in Bismarck. A small percentage of ICE detainments become criminal cases, he said.
Fran Joersz of Bismarck, second from right, smiles while holding a protest sign in front of the William L. Guy Federal Building in Bismarck on Sept. 25, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
During the protest, attendee Rachel Patrie of Bismarck said due process rights are important for those arrested by immigration officers in North Dakota and across the country.
“It is unconstitutional, and I think we have to stand up when things are going wrong in our country,” Patrie said. “I believe that people who are trying to be here legally should be allowed to be here legally, if they are putting in the effort to be here.”
Fran Joersz of Bismarck said she wanted to protest arrests of the Charras workers and also immigration officer-involved shootings in Texas, Maine and Minnesota.
She said she is incredibly proud of the people who are speaking up and standing up for immigrant communities. 
“It just seems like we should have a path to citizenship,” Joersz said. “It’s not my America.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Minburn receives more than $2M to upgrade aging water infrastructure
description: MINBURN – A small, Dallas County community is set to break ground on significant upgrades to its water infrastructure following a $2 million grant and $600,000 loan from U.S. Department of Agriculture Rural Development.  Joe Stuetelberg, the mayor of Minburn, said the city’s current pipes were installed in the 1950s, have “constant” water main-line breaks […[...]
text:
Minburn Iowa's drinking water infrastructure is set to be upgraded with more than $2 million in funding from USDA. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) MINBURN – A small, Dallas County community is set to break ground on significant upgrades to its water infrastructure following a $2 million grant and $600,000 loan from U.S. Department of Agriculture Rural Development. 
Joe Stuetelberg, the mayor of Minburn, said the city’s current pipes were installed in the 1950s, have “constant” water main-line breaks and pressure flows that are so “inadequate” that the volunteer fire department can hardly fight fires in the town and some residents can’t take showers in upstairs bathrooms. 
He said the system also lacks proper valving systems, which means when there is a main break, the city has to “shut the entire town down” and issue boil orders until the repair is completed. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“With the tremendous support of Congressman (Zach) Nunn and his office, as well as the great partnership with the USDA Rural Development office, I’m proud to say that the future generations of Minburn residents will have one less challenge in the coming years,” Stuetelberg said. 
Stuetelberg worked with Nunn’s office to request Community Project Funding for the infrastructure upgrades. The funding request was eventually approved by the House appropriations committee before it could be distributed through the Rural Development office. 
Nunn, speaking in Minburn Friday, said when Stuetelberg came to his office to talk about the grant, his jacket smelled like smoke from working with the volunteer fire department in the city. 
“He was trying to pump out a fire through a two-inch pipe,” Nunn said. “This is the reality: The men and women on the front line for our community, the ones most invested for this, also have to dual hat. Not just being mayor, not just being a fireman, but also making sure that the infrastructure is here for the next generation.” 
The process of getting the grant took several years, during which time Stuetelberg said the city “started raising water rates slowly” to help build the funds for the project which will replace main and distribution lines throughout the city as well as adding necessary valve systems. 
“The citizens are paying, you know, but we obviously can’t afford to charge them $2 million,” Stuetelberg said. 
Stuetelberg said construction is anticipated to begin in the spring.
Minburn Mayor Joe Stuetelberg, left, with Iowa Rural Development Director Mike Sexton at the public library in Minburn, Iowa, Sept. 25, 2026. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Rachel Wacker, executive director for the Greater Dallas County Development Alliance, said the funding will help Minburn provide the “basic infrastructure” that will be “critical” for the city as population continues to increase in the county.
“It’s not just for business attraction or population attraction, these things are very important for the retention of our existing businesses and our existing residents in Minburn,” Wacker said. 
The city of about 320 people gets its water from Xenia Rural Water District, a member of the regional water authority Central Iowa Water Works. 
Tami Madsen, CIWW’s executive director, noted lawn watering restrictions the regional authority has had to exercise the past two summers and said that in Iowa, “water quality and water quantity cannot be separated.” 
“These challenges reinforce why investments in both source water protection and drinking water infrastructure are so important,” Madsen said. “We need to continue improving water quality upstream while also investing in the treatment plants, wells, reservoirs, transmission systems, and other infrastructure necessary to provide reliable drinking water.” 
Nunn, who is running for reelection in a competitive race against Democrat Sarah Trone Garriott, mentioned several water-infrastructure and quality bills he has supported in the House and his efforts to improve groundwater monitoring and lead-pipe replacements in Iowa. 
Recently, the House passed the Water Resources Development Act of 2026, which in part calls for a study of the Saylorville Reservoir, a wetland restoration project in southern Iowa and several Iowa watershed studies. 
USDA Rural Development Under Secretary Glen Smith was also in Minburn for the presentation of funding and noted the ratio of grant to loan awarded to Minburn was “very outstanding.” Typically communities are awarded a large loan and a small grant amount, not the other way around. 
“When people in rural America turn on the tap, they should deserve a clean glass of water,” Smith, who hails from Iowa, said. “That’s exactly what we’re here for, is to provide that real infrastructure, in communities like Minburn, for now, for everyday life and for the future.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: About our lieutenant governor debacle
description: Gov. Mike Sherrill’s administration was thrown into turmoil this week when she accused her lieutenant governor of ethical lapses and demanded his resignation. He complied.
text:
Gov. Mike Sherrill’s administration was thrown into turmoil this week when she accused her lieutenant governor, Dale Caldwell, of ethical lapses and demanded his resignation. He complied.It’s been a whirlwind in Trenton in the last few days, with the Sherrill administration dropping a report on Thursday accusing Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell of multiple ethical lapses and then Caldwell stepping down Friday afternoon, about 1/11 of a Scaramucci later.
I have a few thoughts.
First, while I was initially alarmed by this week’s reports that Gov. Mikie Sherrill left the state more than a dozen times during the Caldwell investigation — leaving him in charge as acting governor — after reading the report, I’m less concerned.
I’m not defending any of his alleged conduct. But the claims in the report amount to making crass remarks to women subordinates, bringing dates to functions without paying for them, and pushing for a promotion for his state worker girlfriend.
If Sherrill had been under the impression that those working with Caldwell were in actual danger or that he could have successfully placed his loved ones on the state payroll, she should have stayed home, but nothing in the report indicates that.
A portion of an investigative report that alleges Lt. Gov. Dale Caldwell made a crass remark to a female subordinate.
The most salacious passage of the report has gotten most of the attention.
It says that a woman who worked for Caldwell alleged that he spent an April function hitting on her much younger friend and that he felt a certain way when she told him on the car ride from the event that the friend was not interested.
Caldwell told her that women their age who are ambitious need a man to help them, according to the report. But, the report alleges he said then, “You young women are looking for young sperm.”
I’m not sure what men still need to hear this in 2026, but if you are in a position of power and talking to a woman subordinate — especially in a place where they cannot easily escape, like a moving car — do not talk about sperm. Unless you’re a medical professional, this is a very easy rule to follow.
The only thing that heartens me about this is that not too long ago, the woman staffer may have felt she couldn’t complain about hearing this crass and inappropriate remark from her much older, more powerful boss. But she told someone and the guy was publicly castigated for it. A tiny bit of progress.
Caldwell denies making this remark. A state trooper who was in the back seat for the car ride said he did not hear this conversation.
Assembly Speaker Craig Coughlin and Senate President Nicholas Scutari speak to reporters during a briefing on Nov. 9, 2023, at the Statehouse in Trenton. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)
The Legislature dodged a bullet when Caldwell decided to resign.
Sherrill did not have a ton of leverage to force Caldwell out, but the Legislature could have voted to remove him.
The most obvious cause for his removal would have been the report’s biggest claim: that Caldwell repeatedly sought a promotion for a state worker he was dating.
In May, Caldwell urged an unnamed state official to promote one of their employees without disclosing that he was dating the woman in question, the report claims.
That same month, Caldwell emailed a second unnamed state official to say the woman he was dating “would be a great addition” to the leadership team at an unnamed state department, the report says.
“I understand there are some openings,” Caldwell wrote. “Please share her information as you see fit.”
The official talked to Caldwell and told him the woman would not be promoted and urged Caldwell to “be careful.” The woman was never promoted and no longer works for the state, the report says.
Caldwell, an outsider who won a landslide election last year after promising to change Trenton’s culture, arrived in our capital and, according to the report’s authors, almost immediately tried to use his influence to benefit his girlfriend. Classic New Jersey.
Caldwell did the Legislature a favor by resigning. If lawmakers had moved forward with trying to remove him, he may have used the proceedings to ask how many of them have procured jobs for their family members or paramours. Would have gotten awkward.
Shirley Emelehu, the state’s comptroller, speaking to reporters after Gov. Mikie Sherrill named her acting secretary of state in Trenton on Sept. 25, 2026. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)
The Caldwell debacle has had one major impact on the public: throwing the office of the secretary of state into turmoil.
Caldwell also served in that role, and as such oversaw our elections. It’s 39 days until Election Day. Mail-in ballots are already in the hands of voters, some of whom have already sent them in. And now Caldwell’s departure has forced Sherrill to put a newcomer into the role of secretary of state, Shirley Emehelu.
This is not a knock on Emehelu, whose career has largely focused on white-collar crime and eight months as our comptroller. But the idea that our state’s elections chief has no experience in that area gives me agita, especially as the Trump administration is moving as swiftly as possible to wholly revamp how our elections are administered.
Sherrill tried to calm those fears when speaking to reporters in Trenton on Friday.
“It is of paramount importance that our elections run smoothly and that New Jerseyans have confidence in the officials overseeing them,” Sherrill said, adding that Emehelu “has the judgment to run these elections and the strength to stand up to Trump’s attacks on voting.”
Here’s hoping Emehelu will be a better choice than Caldwell was.

Republican U.S. Reps. Rick Crawford, French Hill, Steve Womack and Bruce Westerman (courtesy photos)Arkansas’ public television station will host political debates for seven state and federal offices next month, but without Republican U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton.
Cotton’s opponents, Democrat Hallie Shoffner and Libertarian Jeff Wadlin, will debate live at Arkansas TV headquarters in Conway at 1:30 p.m. on Oct. 12. The debate will be rebroadcast at 7 p.m.
Shoffner and Wadlin will also participate in an Oct. 22 debate at ASU-TV, Arkansas State University’s student-led broadcast station in Jonesboro. Cotton will not be present, according to an ASU-TV news release.
Cotton and Shoffner both announced this month that they accepted invitations to a debate hosted by conservative Christian news outlet Salem Media. The date and time have not yet been announced.

Arkansas Republican U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton takes a few questions from media at Republican Party headquarters in downtown Little Rock on March 3, 2026 after being declared winner of his party’s primary. (Photo by John Sykes Jr./Arkansas Advocate)

Cotton participated in the public television network’s debate in his successful 2014 campaign against then-Democratic Sen. Mark Pryor. He opted out of the debate in his 2020 reelection campaign against Libertarian Ricky Dale Harrington. Cotton did not face a Democratic challenger that year.
Republican U.S. Rep. Rick Crawford of the 1st Congressional District will not participate in an Oct. 8 ASU-TV debate against Democrat Terri Yarbrough Green and Libertarian Steve Parsons. The 1st District covers much of north and northeast Arkansas, as well as the Delta.
Crawford will debate both his opponents at Arkansas TV on Oct. 14 at 11 a.m. The debate will be rebroadcast at 6 p.m.
