name: VTDigger
title: Roxbury looks to give its former school a new life
description:
The town took ownership of the building earlier this year and seeks to make it self-sufficient.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Roxbury looks to give its former school a new life.
text:
Roxbury Village School building in Roxbury. Photo credit The Bridge

This story by Tracy Brannstrom was first published in The Bridge on Sept. 22, 2026.
ROXBURY — When the Roxbury Village School closed two years ago, the building didn’t become obsolete. In fact, it remains the town’s largest public gathering space, housing Town Meeting Day, elections, an afterschool program, community meals and other events.
But it comes with a cost. 
The town took ownership of the building earlier this year and has given itself three to five years to make it financially self-sufficient. A seven-member committee appointed in May has been tackling everything from the building’s heating and energy costs to rekeying its doors, fire-code requirements and how to structure rental agreements.
Kristen Getler, chair of the Roxbury Village School Committee, said she is mindful of the town’s tight financial reality. Roxbury has many miles of gravel roads to maintain, she said, and officials are discussing the possibility of a new town garage.
“There is a concern about continuing to carry a building on the town’s operating budget when everybody is feeling pretty stressed with taxes right now, and any added expense has a tax implication,” Getler said. “That’s really real for folks.” 
Roxbury Village School closed in fall 2024 as part of the Montpelier Roxbury Public Schools (MRPS) district effort to cut costs, saving the district $1.5 million, according to Superintendent Libby Bonesteel at the time. Under the merger agreement, the town could buy the building back for $1 if the district could not identify a financially feasible educational use for the roughly 10,000-square-foot space on 2.5 acres.
The town of Roxbury has since spent about $71,000 on operating the building, according to town clerk Tammy Legacy. Legal work related to the property transfer, property insurance, technology upgrades, maintenance and testing for PCBs and other contamination have been among the largest expenses. Fuel is expected to be a major cost this winter, and the town is also considering replacing the building’s fuel tank, Legacy said. 
The town will budget somewhere between $50,000 and $100,000 for the building in the coming year, said Roxbury selectboard chair Jeremy Reed, who also said the building committee is putting together financial projections to put before voters on Town Meeting Day in March.
The hope for those involved in redeveloping the building is to maximize rental revenue in the coming years. The committee identified 4,673 square feet of potentially rentable space that could generate roughly $68,000 to $115,000 a year, depending on rates. 
Though a former owner of the building, MRPS is now the town’s first major tenant. In early September, the building committee finalized a lease for the district to host its afterschool program, expected to bring in about $15,000 through next June, although that revenue is not guaranteed beyond the current agreement. 
Reed said the Vermont Farm and Forest School, an independent K–5 private school and outdoor education program in Roxbury, is another possible tenant that’s conducting its own feasibility study to run an early-childhood program in the building. In fact, a number of childcare facilities and a private school showed interest in renting space, but Roxbury’s rural location is challenging, Reed added. 
The town also hopes to secure grants to help offset the building’s costs in the coming years. 
Asked if the building might pay for itself, Reed said, “I think there’s a hope that can be the outcome, but it does sound like there’s been a bit of a realization that (it) will be harder than we thought.”
But before the town can lease more space, it has to clear out the building. The attic is packed with items the school district left behind, including boxes of unopened, unused curricula, while the library is overflowing with books the town library has no room to house, said building committee secretary Heidi Albright. 
“We’re trying to figure out how to afford fuel and replace an oil tank, and we have this mundane project of dealing with all these castoffs that the district didn’t want to deal with,” Albright said. 
“There is a little bit of a sense that we got the fuzzy end of the lolly pop.”
Albright said she remains optimistic about what the former school building could become, but getting there has required a lot of work behind the scenes. Juggling the building committee with her Third Branch Flower farm, family life and other obligations is difficult, she said.
“In a small town, you basically have a small group of people who do so much, because they care so much, then they really burn out.”
Albright would like to see the town hire someone to assist with coordinating the work around repurposing the building, although that may not be financially feasible.
Alyssa Johnson, a program manager at the Vermont Council on Rural Development, an organization supporting Roxbury’s redevelopment efforts since spring 2025, agreed that much of the work of repurposing schools and other community buildings in Vermont falls on the backs of under-resourced volunteers.
“There just isn’t a coordinated wraparound system of support in the state for this,” Johnson said. “It tends to be a very patchwork approach, often involving communities that are the smallest and have the fewest paid staff to help support the work.” 
Support from the council and Preservation Trust Vermont, which often work together, has been critical, several residents serving on the building committee said. 
Last fall, both organizations took a taskforce of Roxbury residents around the state to see properties undergoing repurposing, including a former Bridgewater elementary school that closed in 2015 that was converted into a community and childcare center in 2021. 
Prior to the bus tour, in 2025, the Council on Rural Development facilitated three public forums in Roxbury for residents to discuss what they wanted for the town’s future, with repurposing the elementary school identified as a priority.
Preservation Trust president Ben Doyle, who is also a Montpelier city councilor, said more than two dozen communities in Vermont are grappling with how to use shuttered schools. The buildings range from large high schools to one-room schoolhouses, and from century-old structures to those built in the 1950s and ’60s. Their condition, size and layout can shape what comes next, from housing to community centers.
Doyle said Vermont’s push under Act 73 toward newer and fewer schools raises the question of what happens to all the shuttered schools left behind.
“What are we going to do with these community assets that are kind of like, left there? They don’t just go away, right?”
He said these buildings offer towns and residents an opportunity to think about how to play a role in local economic development.
In Roxbury — population 678, according to the 2020 census — the former elementary school has already emerged as a potential asset for development. The question is how to make it work.
For now, the building hosts free community events from two nonprofits that formed in the aftermath of the school’s closure. Roxbury Roots currently hosts a grant-funded series of Sunday workshops on local food production, and Roxbury Rising will hold its second annual silent disco in November.
Under the merger agreement between the town and MRPS, the building must be used for community purposes for at least five years after the town takes ownership.
Getler, who runs Moonlight Mountain Farm in Roxbury, got involved with community uses of the building almost immediately after the school’s closure. She was serving on the MRPS board when it made the decision, and voted against it, a contentious process she said left residents without a say.
With the building’s future still largely uncertain, she still sees a way for the old school to remain part of the community.
“I see that kids have a thread keeping them tied to Roxbury,” she said, referring to how the town’s elementary students now attend school at Union Elementary School in Montpelier.
“And overall, people are accessing the building in ways they never have before.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Roxbury looks to give its former school a new life.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Nebraska hits trifecta in federal grant awards for child welfare system
description: LINCOLN — Nebraska’s Department of Health and Human Services has been selected to receive nearly $1.5 million in federal grants intended to modernize the child welfare system. The funds come in three grants from the Administration for Children and Families, a division of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. A state DHHS spokesperson […]
text:
A mother and her son hold hands on a swing set. Nebraska received three grants to upgrade child welfare related operations. (Photo by Troy Bennett/Maine Morning Star)LINCOLN — Nebraska’s Department of Health and Human Services has been selected to receive nearly $1.5 million in federal grants intended to modernize the child welfare system.
The funds come in three grants from the Administration for Children and Families, a division of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.
A state DHHS spokesperson said Friday that Nebraska was the only state to qualify for all three of the grants. 
No new staff are to be hired, said Jeff Powell, the agency spokesman. He said some of the funding could offset the public agency’s administrative costs, and the bulk will build or enhance infrastructure for existing and new programs.
Alyssa Bish, director of the division of children and family services in the Nebraska Department of Health and Human Services. (Courtesy of DHHS)
One award of $137,240 is to update licensing procedures, including fingerprinting, background checks and other systems used to license caregivers and foster families. Nebraska was one of 14 jurisdictions nationwide to receive that grant.
“By expanding access to fingerprinting and improving how information moves through the system, we can reduce unnecessary delays and better support relatives, kin and other caregivers who step forward when a child needs a safe home,” said Kathleen Stolz, deputy director of the department’s children and family services division. 
That grant builds on the other two:
Nebraska was selected as one of 10 jurisdictions that each received nearly $600,000 for a “predictive analytics in child welfare” pilot program. The emerging technology is aimed at improving child safety and caseworker decision-making. It taps historical data and algorithms to identify patterns and estimate the probability of outcomes such as child maltreatment risk.
Nebraska also was among a select group of 10 states awarded a Title IV-E “prevention accelerator” grant. With that $750,000 grant, the state  is expected to strengthen referral pathways and prevention services. 
“Each of these investments strengthens a different part of Nebraska’s child welfare system, but they are connected by a common goal of helping children and families get the right support at the right time,” said Alyssa Bish, director of children and family services.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Jolly to national Democrats:  Show me some money
description: TAMPA — With more polls and election analysts suggesting David Jolly could become the first Democrat to win a governor’s race in Florida in more than three decades, the former GOP congressman is appealing for money to defeat Republican Byron Donalds. This week the national elections rating group Decision Desk HQ shifted the Florida governor’s race […]
text:
Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Jolly speaking at the Tampa Tiger Bay Club in Ybor City's Cuban Club on Sept. 25, 2026 (Photo by Don Kruse for the Florida Phoenix)TAMPA — With more polls and election analysts suggesting David Jolly could become the first Democrat to win a governor’s race in Florida in more than three decades, the former GOP congressman is appealing for money to defeat Republican Byron Donalds.
This week the national elections rating group Decision Desk HQ shifted the Florida governor’s race to a “Toss up,” saying Donalds has a 60% probability of winning, down from 68%.
Speaking to several hundred people who gathered in Tampa’s Ybor City for a Tiger Bay  Club forum, Jolly was asked about what it was going to take to convince the majority of the electorate he is the better candidate to take the state forward over the next four years.
“I need the national Democratic Party to come into Florida and start spending money,” he said to cheers, repeating what he said was a claim by a top Tallahassee Republican consultant that the only way he could lose is “if the national Democrats chose to take a pass on Florida like they have in the past 10 years.”
Jolly has acknowledged he was never going to outraise Donalds for campaign contributions, but the money gap is widening as much as the polls are tightening. Donalds has now raised more than $115 million via his political committee, while Jolly has raised $15.8 million, combining his regular and political committee campaign accounts.
“If the national party doesn’t come, I worry about this race,” Jolly told reporters following his one-hour appearance.
“I don’t mean to punch at Byron, but $75 to $100 million used on lies can be effective,” he added. “If we lose this race because Byron’s able to convince voters of something that’s not true, when all we need is a little bit from national Democrats to come in and shore up this race, arguably prosecute the case against Byron, I’m not going to have the resources to do that.”
That tune is different than what Jolly was singing from a month ago.
On the eve of the Aug. 18 primary, Jolly said that while he didn’t want to be “naïve” about financial resources to remain competitive, “this is a cycle where you can get outspent 10 to one and still win.”  He added, “I think we’re going to see money come in.”
Hillsborough County state Sen. Brian Nathan was one Democrat outspent roughly 10:1 when he defeated Republican Josie Tomkow in a special election in Hillsborough County in March, but that race was relegated to one county, not a state with more than 13.5 million registered voters.
Some Democratic strategists are skeptical national Democratic dollars will flow to Florida.
“If you keep waiting on national, it’ll never come,” Democratic fundraising strategist Jackson McMillan wrote in a social media post Friday. “Build up your grassroots apparatus instead, your small $ program should be so much better than it is!”
Decision on not debating is ‘final’
One way Jolly could get his message out would be a debate with Donalds, but the Democrat announced Sunday he would not do so this cycle.
Jolly was asked by one member in the audience to reconsider, saying it was his “duty” to do so.
Jolly disagreed, declaring firmly that his decision was “final.”
He repeated comments he made earlier this week that he didn’t want to “platform” a candidate in Donalds, who he says has “lied” about his platform, and that he wants to lead by example to his two young children about “elevating our politics to something better, not into driving us into further division and vitriol.”
Who has the better plan on property insurance?
One of his policy positions that Jolly says Donalds is lying about is the latter’s contention that his plan on property insurance would constitute a “$1,000 tax” — as Donalds-sponsored ads have said on television for weeks now.
Donalds has based his statements by alluding to a report from Florida State University about a plan introduced by a bipartisan pair of Florida lawmakers in 2024. (That plan is not publicly available but was shared with the Phoenix by the Donalds campaign.)
Jolly acknowledged to reporters that his plan is “a bold initiative” but would need to go before voters as a constitutional amendment to be approved.
“I can’t do it by executive action, but the reality is, Florida homeowners feel more anxious than they do secure about the homeowners insurance market,” he said.
Donalds released his “Bring Down the Bill” property insurance proposal earlier this month, which would maintain legislation passed by the GOP-led Legislature in 2022 and 2023. The Donalds campaign says those laws have reduced insurance lawsuits and in turn “helped lower insurance companies’ legal costs and resulted in lower homeowners insurance premiums.”
Jolly contends that’s simply more of what’s going on right now, and he says homeowners are not satisfied with the status quo.
He may be right about that. In what is being labeled a “landmark survey” of 1,511 Florida property insurance policyholders published Friday by the Orlando Sentinel, South Florida Sentinel, and the University of North Florida’s Public Opinion Research Lab, 55% of those surveyed saw no signs the insurance market is improving and 26% said it it is getting worse.

name: Washington State Standard
title: To train and retain Washington’s future doctors, look to local med school, clinic partnerships
description: Preparing the next generation of doctors to serve Washington communities will take a coordinated, cross-sector, long-term strategy, a family medicine doctor argues.
text:
Washington state needs to do more to boost the supply of medical doctors, a family medicine doctor argues. (Getty Images)How can we make sure that Washington has a strong pipeline of future doctors to care for our communities?
Whether you’re an Evergreen State doctor, a young person interested in medicine, a parent, a patient, or a policymaker, that question is central to the future of healthcare in our state.
As a doctor who helps train the next generation of Washington physicians, I see what’s at stake every day: when patients wait too long to see a doctor, manageable health concerns can become much more serious. Washington faces a growing shortage of primary care doctors, especially in rural and underserved communities. Stronger partnerships between our state’s medical schools and community clinicians are one way to solve this challenge and help future doctors train in our communities.
The need for more doctors is stark and growing
By 2030, Washington will face a shortage of more than 6,000 doctors, including nearly 1,700 primary care providers. Every one of Washington’s counties – from Spokane to Walla Walla to Pierce to Grays Harbor – currently has “health professional shortage areas,” defined as 3,500 or more patients for every one provider. Twenty-one communities here have fewer than one doctor per 10,000 people, putting Washington in the bottom half of the country for doctor availability.
This doctor shortage disproportionately affects our rural communities. In 2023, 25 of Washington’s 39 counties each had less than 1% of the state’s practicing doctors. Fewer local providers can mean longer waits, longer drives and delayed care, which can push patients toward more expensive urgent or emergency care. That lack of access has economic consequences, too, making it harder for employers in affected areas to recruit and retain workers.
Washington has already taken some important steps to fill the gap, such as providing preceptorship grants to nurse practitioners who agree to teach in a clinical setting and expanding access to virtual or telehealth appointments.
However, we need to do more — and that starts with connecting future providers with the communities where they’re needed.
Connecting future providers with communities where they’re needed
Our organization partnered with Washington State University — home to one of just three medical schools in our state — to help future doctors get in-clinic experience in communities in our state, build ties with patients, and then stay to serve those very same communities.
In our partnership, WSU medical students spend nearly a year immersed in hands-on, clinical learning with mentorship from Optum Care Washington doctors in clinics across King and Snohomish County. Where traditional training often moves students discipline by discipline through hospital-based rotations, these students learn multiple disciplines simultaneously in community-based outpatient clinics, working alongside Optum doctors as they care for patients over time.
This approach benefits patients, who can develop a relationship with a consistent care team; students, who gain exposure to the continuity of care they will experience as residents and practicing doctors; and clinics across Washington, which are connected with future talent. And, we prioritize these relationships when recruiting and hiring future residents and doctors.
Preparing the next generation of doctors to serve Washington communities will take a coordinated, cross-sector, long-term strategy. One of the most impactful steps we can take now is to expand and scale programs that recruit, train, and retain future doctors in Washington communities that need them most. Our leaders in Olympia have an opportunity to expand investments in residency programs, with a focus on primary care for Washington communities that need the next generation of health care providers the most.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kansas attorney general orders League of Women Voters to stop paying teens to register to vote
description: Kansas attorney general tells League of Women Voters in Leavenworth County to stop offering $5 gift cards to high school students registering to vote.
text:
Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach issued a letter to force the League of Women Voters of Leavenworth County to stop violating state and federal law by giving $5 gift cards to high school students who register to vote. (Photo by Tim Carpenter/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — Attorney General Kris Kobach sent a cease-and-desist letter Friday to the League of Women Voters to stop violations of state and federal law by offering financial incentives to high school students who registered to vote.
The issue surfaced after state Rep. Pat Proctor, a Leavenworth Republican, complained about voter registration campaigns during May at Lansing and Leavenworth high schools. The Leavenworth County chapter of the League of Women Voters had promoted distribution of $5 Starbucks gift cards to students who registered.
In a statement, Kobach said he referred the matter to the U.S. attorney in Kansas for investigation.
In elections with a federal candidate on the ballot, U.S. law prohibits an individual, nonprofit or labor union from paying or offering to pay a person to register to vote or to cast a ballot. Federal law doesn’t ban free rides to the polls or providing employees paid leave to vote.
“Paying people to register or to vote is illegal, period,” Kobach said. “The size of the gift card does not matter.”
The penalty under federal law featured a maximum fine of $10,000 and a prison sentence up to five years.
The attorney general said the prohibition in both Kansas and U.S. law was designed to “protect the integrity of our elections and public confidence in the results.”
The attorney general’s office reserved the right to take enforcement action in the future against the League of Women Voters, he said.
“Groups may encourage registration and help eligible Kansans complete the process. They may not buy registrations,” Kobach said.
The attorney general’s cease-and-desist letter sent  to the League of Women Voters of Leavenworth County and the League of Women Voters of Kansas called for a halt to offering cash, gift cards or anything else of value to register people to vote.
The document directed the county chapter to preserve financial records and registration forms related to its incentive program involving high school students. In addition, Kobach asked the chapter to respond within 30 days with information identifying every instance in which the organization distributed cash or gift cards in exchange for a person voting or registering to vote.
The League of Women Voters of Leavenworth County brought attention to their unusual effort to register young voters by posting photographs on Facebook. One post included a sign that said, “Register to vote get a $5 Starbucks gift card.”
Proctor, the House Elections Committee chairman, is a candidate for secretary of state. He’s running against Democrat Jennifer Day in the Nov. 3 election. Secretary of State Scott Schwab chose not to seek reelection.
Proctor encouraged Kobach to launch an inquiry but asked the attorney general not to investigate students who may have accepted illegal payments to register or to vote.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: South Dakota’s long, strange trip with Monae Johnson
description: Recent events have some South Dakota Republicans questioning the integrity of “election integrity” enthusiast Monae Johnson. This happened after the secretary of state endorsed a Democrat who’s running for election to her office. Johnson’s election as secretary of state and her tenure there has been a long, strange trip. At the 2022 Republican convention, sh[...]
text:
South Dakota Secretary of State Monae Johnson speaks during a press conference about election security and integrity on Oct. 9, 2024, at the University of Nebraska at Omaha. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)Recent events have some South Dakota Republicans questioning the integrity of “election integrity” enthusiast Monae Johnson. This happened after the secretary of state endorsed a Democrat who’s running for election to her office.
Johnson’s election as secretary of state and her tenure there has been a long, strange trip. At the 2022 Republican convention, she unseated incumbent Steve Barnett by disparaging as too risky his emphasis on technology to implement online voting and online voter registration. Johnson promised an emphasis on election integrity with her supporters putting an emphasis on hand-counting ballots.
That year, South Dakotans elected an election denier to run their elections. Johnson staunchly refused to say if Joe Biden had defeated Donald Trump in the 2020 election.
Johnson must have felt a sense of deja vu at this year’s Republican convention as election integrity advocates turned against her. She was jettisoned in favor of Heather Baxter, a candidate whose website said at the time she was in favor of hand-counting ballots. Johnson’s downfall at the convention can likely be attributed to this quote from her speech to delegates: “I trust the county auditors and I fully support the use of secure, tested ballot tabulators.”
South Dakota’s top election official, a Republican, endorses a Democrat to succeed her

If she is elected, Baxter will learn what Johnson already knows. There’s a big difference between being a voting integrity advocate and being secretary of state. Baxter made Johnson’s perceived shortcomings in the area of voting integrity the main reason why convention delegates should put Baxter on the ballot instead. What Baxter ignored, at her own peril, is the full scale of tasks for which the secretary of state has responsibility. In addition to the Division of Elections, the secretary of state oversees responsibilities as vast as they are diverse, including but not limited to: annual reports for businesses, trademarks, pistol permits and information about lobbyists. Obviously there’s more to the job than wrangling county auditors.
If she ascends to the office, Baxter is likely to find that the legislators in her own party are not nearly as enthusiastic about hand-counting ballots as were the delegates at the Republican convention. Lawmakers are also politicians. Many of them, as good Republicans, probably have discrete “election integrity” tattoos. As politicians, the last thing they want to do on Election Day is wait around all night for results.
Hand-counting ballots would add hours to the process in small towns and add days to getting results in the state’s larger communities. In an age of instant gratification, waiting around for election results isn’t in our DNA. No matter what they have said about election integrity in the past, Republican lawmakers will be hesitant about going back to the wild west days when men were men and ballots were counted by hand.
Another lesson headed Baxter’s way is that integrity isn’t lacking in South Dakota elections. While the election process is far-flung and can be complicated, in this state it is largely free of fraud. Hand-counting — another term for adding the propensity for human error to the process — certainly won’t make our elections any safer or the tally more accurate.
[Voter Guide: 2026 general election Voter Guide: The candidates, the ballot measures, and the tools you need to cast your vote.]
Johnson’s endorsement of Democrat Terrence Davis sparked some chatter about her embrace of proven election methods and her casting off the foolishness inherent in those who cry out for more election integrity without evidence that our elections need improvement. While her philosophy may be changing, that doesn’t alter the fact that her tenure as secretary of state has been a bumpy one:

Her implementation of new voter registration laws was so ham-handed that it sparked a lawsuit.
Her office was a little too transparent when it accidentally outed thousands of people on public assistance while publishing voter information.
Her office mishandled early voting in the June primary, which ended up starting late.
Her office incorrectly told independent candidates that they needed hundreds more signatures to get on the ballot than they actually did.
In keeping with a trait that’s far too prevalent in state government, her office is noted for standing by mute when there is a request for information from the press.

Obviously Johnson was better at getting her job than she was at keeping it. She’s a politician who agitated her way into the secretary of state’s office. She knows how to make waves and she whipped up a tsunami by endorsing a Democrat.
With a list of flubs and mistakes to her credit, maybe getting passed over at the convention was a blessing in disguise. The next secretary of state will be comforted by the notion that Johnson certainly has not set the bar too high.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: At least 10 people detained at Columbus County checkpoint, NC advocacy group says
description: At least 10 people were arrested or detained Thursday evening during a license checkpoint operation in Tabor City, according to Siembra NC, an immigrant rights advocacy group.  The checkpoint took place near N.C. Highway 904 and Pireway Road between about 5:30 and 7 p.m., Siembra NC said.  Video obtained by the group shows a man […]
text:
Several hundred gathered at Moore Square in downtown Raleigh on Tuesday, Nov. 18, 2025 to protest ongoing ICE and U.S. Border Patrol raids in Charlotte and the Research Triangle area. (Photo: Galen Bacharier/NC Newsline)At least 10 people were arrested or detained Thursday evening during a license checkpoint operation in Tabor City, according to Siembra NC, an immigrant rights advocacy group. 
The checkpoint took place near N.C. Highway 904 and Pireway Road between about 5:30 and 7 p.m., Siembra NC said. 
Video obtained by the group shows a man wearing a badge standing near two men sitting in the grass next to a road. The seated men’s hands are behind their backs. 
https://ncnewsline.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/2026-09-25_Siembra.mp4
Multiple witnesses told the organization that Latino drivers were asked where they were born, and people who could not produce state identification were arrested. Witnesses also reported that passengers, not just drivers, were questioned about their immigration status and asked to provide citizenship documents, and some were detained.
Javier Carbajal, an electrician who encountered the checkpoint while driving home with his coworkers, said he presented his driver’s license but was ordered out of his car and patted down by a sheriff’s deputy. 
He said a passenger in his car was also questioned about his documents and was arrested after he couldn’t produce them. 
“We are electricians. We were just coming home after a long day of work,” he said. 
Carbajal also reported seeing multiple other people put inside a van. Two other witnesses told Siembra NC they saw Latino men on the side of the road with their hands in zip ties. 
ICE expected to open mass detention facility in NC, sparking anger, pushback

As of Friday, several families who contacted the advocacy group were still trying to determine where their family members had been taken. Families reported contacting detention centers in Onslow, Columbus and New Hanover counties without finding some of the detainees, Siembra NC said. 
The Columbus County Sheriff’s Office participates in the federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement Agency’s 287(g) Task Force, which allows local law enforcement to perform some federal immigration enforcement tasks with ICE supervision. 
The sheriff’s office declined to confirm the checkpoint or the arrests. The office said it could not release information because it was part of an ongoing investigation. 
The incident follows a similar checkpoint in Tabor City earlier this month, when Siembra NC said at least three people encountered by law enforcement were moved into ICE custody. 
The organization said it’s continuing to document Thursday’s arrests and is working to determine where detainees were taken and which agencies were involved.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Top U.S. Senate Republican stumps with Collins in Georgia as seat appears to slip out of reach
description: U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune came to Atlanta to keep hope alive for the Mike Collins campaign as Collins challenges Democratic U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff in the Nov. 3 midterm election. Thune’s visit came amid reports that national Republicans are deprioritizing Georgia’s Senate race in favor of states they feel they have a better […]
text:
Senate Majority Leader John Thune speaks at a Mike Collins event in Atlanta on Sept. 25, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderU.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune came to Atlanta to keep hope alive for the Mike Collins campaign as Collins challenges Democratic U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff in the Nov. 3 midterm election.
Thune’s visit came amid reports that national Republicans are deprioritizing Georgia’s Senate race in favor of states they feel they have a better shot of winning, like Texas, Maine, Alaska, Ohio, Michigan and New Hampshire.
Pollsters give Ossoff a sizable lead, with the Real Clear Politics polling average placing him nearly eight points ahead of Collins, 51.1% to 43.3%, and the Cook Political Report this week changed its rating for the race from “lean Democrat” to “likely Democrat.”
But speaking with reporters at a Buckhead cafe Friday, Thune said the Senate Republican caucus believes the Trump-endorsed Collins has a shot at becoming its next member.
Republican U.S. Senate candidate Mike Collins speaks at a Georgia Chamber event in Athens, Aug. 5, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
“I wouldn’t be here if I didn’t think that we could win the state of Georgia,” the South Dakota Republican said. “It’s going to come down to who gets out to vote on Election Day, and there’s been a significant investment made now in ensuring that we turn our voters out on Election Day.”
Thune also appeared with Collins at a closed-door fundraiser Thursday night featuring Gov. Brian Kemp and other top Georgia Republicans. Kemp had previously supported Collins’ opponent in the GOP primary and cast doubts on Collins’ ability to win in a general election.
Thune’s PAC, Senate Leadership Fund, reported spending $1.7 million this week on ads opposing Ossoff, part of a nearly $4.5 million expenditure in Georgia, Michigan, Maine and Iowa’s U.S. senate races.
So far, Senate Leadership Fund and the associated One Nation nonprofit have spent $25.9 million in the Georgia race, and the fund has an additional $17.3 million in television ad reservations in the state, according to the Collins campaign.
All those dollars could be a big help to Collins in a race where Ossoff has had a strong financial edge.
During the last fundraising reporting period, Ossoff was the top political fundraiser in the country, according to the Federal Election Commission, entering into the current reporting period with $42 million on hand. Collins’ report showed a relatively meager warchest containing $2.2 million.
“It takes resources to communicate, no question about it,” Thune said Friday. “It’s an expensive state, especially in the Atlanta market, but we’re doing everything we can to get resources in this direction, and we believe that Mike Collins is going to win here.”
Collins said flipping the seat won by Ossoff in early 2021 was always going to be a tough battle, but he expressed confidence that Georgians would learn about the candidates over the coming weeks and find Ossoff’s record too liberal.
Georgia Republican Party Chairman Josh McKoon. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
“It’s the number one race in the country,” he said. “Jon Ossoff has been the most vulnerable Democrat out there, period, and it is because of the way he votes. You’ve got a crystal clear choice in this race.”
Georgia GOP Chairman Josh McKoon said the key to a Collins win will be mobilizing the coalition that helped President Donald Trump win the state in 2024 even though Trump is not on the ballot this year.
“We’ve got hundreds of thousands of voters that voted for Donald Trump in 2024 that have never voted in a midterm election, and at the Georgia Republican Party, we are laser focused on getting those people off the couch and in the voting booth,” McKoon said Friday. “If we turn those people out, we’re gonna win these elections.”
Speaking to reporters during a virtual press conference Thursday, Ossoff expressed confidence that voters would find Collins too distasteful to elect to the U.S. Senate in large part because of his connections to Trump.
U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff at an Atlanta rally Aug. 16, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
“Congressman Mike Collins is a Trump puppet who has voted seven times for the disastrous Iran war that has sent gas prices through the roof,” Ossoff said. “He’s voted repeatedly for the Trump tariffs that sent grocery prices soaring, and he voted with Donald Trump to double health insurance premiums for more than a million Georgians. He possesses not a shred of independence. He is Donald Trump’s puppet, and we will be sure to remind voters of that over the next 40 days.”
Ossoff cited scandals that have rocked Collins’ campaign, including an House ethics investigation into allegations that his office used government funds to pay a top aide’s girlfriend for work she didn’t do, antisemitic videos from his son-in-law, apparent efforts from another top aide to intervene on behalf of an associate who had minimized the extent of the Holocaust who had been jailed for contempt of court and bizarre posts from another former staffer, including an image of the staffer wearing Ku Klux Klan robes and of a swastika made out of the word “twink.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Blumenthal, Lamont: Trump blocking CT grants for political reasons
description: A judge ruled the Trump administration illegally halted $53 million in clean energy grants for CT recipients. They have yet to be released.
text:
U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal and Gov. Ned Lamont complained Friday that the Trump administration has yet to release federal energy grants terminated a year ago on the basis of whether the recipients were in states won by Kamala Harris in 2024 and are represented by Democratic senators. 
“It’s illogical, illegal, intolerable — and that’s in effect what the court found. The district court in the District of Columbia held that this cancelation of grants was in fact illegal, but the administration has not yet provided them,” Blumenthal said at a press conference in Hartford.
In stipulated judgments issued in January and June on cases challenging the termination a year ago of $7.6 billion in clean energy grants, U.S. District Judge Amit P. Mehta concluded the administration had acted illegally. While applying only to a portion of the grants, the decisions addressed motivation for all the cancellations.
One dozen of the 284 terminated grants were slated for eight recipients in Connecticut, including the University of Connecticut and RTX, the corporate parent of Pratt & Whitney. RTX was the recipient of four of the 12 grants. Blumenthal said the grants owed to Connecticut recipients was $53 million.
The complaint voiced Friday was not new but rather an update on a standoff that persists despite the two court decisions and lobbying by senators.
Blumenthal was one of 37 senators to sign a letter on July 30 urging Energy Secretary Chris Wright to release grants awarded by the Biden administration and blocked at the instigation of federal budget director Russell Vought, who boasted on social media that “the Left’s climate agenda is being canceled.” 
The senator said Mehta’s conclusions have been ignored, not challenged.
“There’s no excuse for this administration disobeying the law and withholding this funding,” Blumenthal said.
“It’s amazing how brazen the Trump administration is — ‘We’re cutting off this basic research funding because we don’t like you, and you’re from a blue state,’” Lamont said. 
Mehta, who sits on the U.S. District Court in Washington, ruled in June on a case brought by a coalition of plaintiffs led by the American Institute of Chemical Engineers. The decision in June specifically applied to at least some of the Connecticut grantees.
Lawyers for the administration signed off on stipulations in two cases before Mehta and another in northern California in which they concede blue state recipients had been targeted. They initially defended it as a move to protect taxpayers against wasteful spending.
“DOE accepts that the inclusion of grants in the October notice tranche was based solely on the political identity of the grant recipient’s state,” the stipulation stated. With one exception, the 284 terminated grants had a had a connection to “a state that awarded its electoral votes to Kamala Harris in the 2024 election and has two Democratic-caucusing Senators.” 
The stipulation was first reported by the New York Times.
But a DOE spokesperson said in a statement Friday, “None of the termination decisions were based on political considerations.” 
Blumenthal and Lamont spoke Friday at a press conference with Emma Cimino, the acting state commissioner of energy and environmental protection, and Rep. Jaime Foster, D-Ellington, a scientist and member of the legislature’s Energy and Technology Committee.
“It is a frustrating time to be a leader in the energy policy space and to be a research scientist,” Foster said. “It is very clear that the way that we do research and development in this country is heavily reliant on federal investment, and when there is uncertainty in the way to fund future research, research teams lose really important time in developing their teams’ processes as they move forward.”
Cimino said Connecticut is particularly sensitive to the federal action.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal and Emma Cimino, the acting commissioner of energy and environmental protection.  Credit: Mark Pazniokas / ctmirror.org

“We’re at the forefront of research and development on emerging technologies, with many of the amazing companies located in our state, the elite universities doing a lot of this research,” Cimino said. “And these actions by the Trump administration hurt those companies. They hurt our researchers, and they don’t position us for success amid a constantly and rapidly changing energy landscape.”
The Department of Energy did not answer specific questions about the status of the 12 Connecticut grants.
Besides UConn and RTX, the other grant recipients in Connecticut are Karpman Consulting, Proton Energy Systems, FuelCell Energy, Mott Corporation, Linde PLC and Calcify.
The $10 million grant to the Mott Corporation, based in Farmington, was for the development of titanium parts used in fuel cells. UConn and an Wallingford company, Nel Hydrogen, also was involved, according to a DOE document.
RTX was the recipient for four of grants totaling more than $14 million to help develop advanced combustion turbines, as well as composite tanks for the storage of liquid hydrogen. 
Linde PLC, the German gas and engineering company, had been awarded $9.5 million to develop a hydrogen refueling station for heavy-duty trucks. That work was to take place at the company’s facilities in Danbury, Oklahoma and Texas, according to project documents. 
The University of Connecticut was to receive $2.25 million. 
Unclear was whether the recipients had received partial payments before the cutoff ordered in October, nine months after Trump returned to the White House and put Vought in charge of the Office of Management and Budget.
Blumenthal said he hoped Republican senators would help bring pressure on the administration for a resolution.
“The idea that the administration is continuing to disobey the court and illegally withhold these funds should be abhorrent to Republicans as well as Democrats, because what goes around comes around,” he said. “They ought to be as fearful of political retribution when it comes to blue states as it would be to red states if Democrats were doing this kind of illegal action.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi attendance law brings new rules for student absences
authors: Allyson Cole, RHCJC and Gaven Wallace, RHCJC
description: An empty classroom at Bailey APAC Middle School in Jackson, Miss., on Friday, July 18, 2025.
text:
As Mississippi public school districts update attendance policies under a new state law, some parents, educators and health care providers are questioning how the changes will affect students who miss school because of illness.
Senate Bill 2103, which took effect July 1, requires public school districts to adopt locally tailored attendance policies by Nov. 1 as part of a statewide effort to reduce chronic absenteeism.
The law generally allows students five excused absences per semester. For illness or injury, medical documentation is required after a student’s third illness-related absence. Superintendents or their designees can approve additional excused absences for extenuating circumstances, including prolonged illness supported by medical documentation.
Constance Barnes-Woods, a pediatrician at Beanstalk Pediatrics, said the requirements should account for students with chronic illnesses.
“We support every effort to have children in the classroom, but we also like to see some flexibility with those children who have chronic illnesses,” Barnes-Woods said.
Constance Barnes-Woods
She pointed to sickle cell disease as one example, saying children can experience unpredictable complications and sometimes require extended hospital stays.
“We see patients with sickle cell anemia. It’s lifelong,” Barnes-Woods said. “They cannot predict, unfortunately, when they’re going to get sick.”
Shayla Haynes, a mother and educator in Monticello, said she supports efforts to address absenteeism.
“Speaking as a teacher, it’s good that they do have that plan in place because there are some students that just don’t come to school, and not because it’s their fault, because their parents just won’t send them,” Haynes said.
But Haynes said illness presents a different concern. Her son has asthma and allergies that do not always require medical treatment.
“If he has like an allergy or asthma flare-up, I don’t take him to the doctor. I just keep him at home because I know what it is,” Haynes said.
Requiring documentation after repeated illnesses could mean additional medical visits.
“I could take him to the doctor, but it’ll be a blank trip because I know what it is,” Haynes said.
Barnes-Woods said children with minor illnesses do not necessarily need medical treatment. A child with mild cold symptoms who is otherwise eating, drinking and behaving normally may be able to recover at home, she said.
She said the documentation requirement could also encourage some families to seek care they otherwise would not.
“To an extent I see it as positive because some parents would just self-treat at home,” Barnes-Woods said. “But if they know that a doctor’s excuse is required, that does prompt them to come and seek medical attention to ensure accurate diagnosis.”
For other families, obtaining documentation can present financial and logistical challenges. Depending on insurance, families may face copays, while uninsured patients may have to pay out of pocket. Parents may also struggle to find same-day appointments, arrange transportation or leave work.
“I have parents that are afraid of losing their jobs when they come multiple times for sick children,” Barnes-Woods said.
Barnes-Woods said parents have told her they have missed children’s routine medical appointments because they could not miss school or work or lacked transportation.
Her clinic has had days this school year when 40% to 50% of scheduled patients did not show up for appointments, she said. The rate varies significantly from day to day, and Barnes-Woods said concerns about missing school may be one factor.
Barnes-Woods said she would like districts to use the law’s flexibility for students with documented chronic conditions.
“I would suggest that children with chronic illnesses like asthma, sick cell disease and some other diseases be exempt from that policy,” she said.
The changes come as Mississippi continues to struggle with chronic absenteeism.
The Mississippi Department of Education reported 27.6% of public school students were chronically absent during the 2024-25 school year, up from 24.4% the previous year. MDE defines chronic absenteeism as missing at least 10% of enrolled school days for any reason, including excused and unexcused absences and suspensions.
Chronic absenteeism declined among elementary and middle school students during the 2024-25 school year but increased among high school students from 30% to 39%, according to MDE.
The new requirements establish earlier interventions intended to address absences before they become more serious.
After three cumulative absences, whether excused or unexcused, schools must contact the student’s parent or guardian, document the communication and begin school-based interventions. Five cumulative unlawful absences trigger a referral to a school attendance officer, with additional referrals required as unlawful absences accumulate.
Bryan Marshall, associate state superintendent, said schools will need different approaches depending on the students they serve.
“The effectiveness of the strategy is going to depend on the age of the child,” Marshall said. “What works in a high school is not going to work in elementary, so to say there’s a blanket intervention, there’s not, and there’s no magic bullet for attendance.”
Bryan Marshall, associate state superintendent
If school-based interventions do not work, districts can turn to outside services.
“Once the interventions are put in place, if those are not working, then we have to get a third-party intervention with some sort of family counseling or whatever the district chooses in their area,” Marshall said.
The law also raises the portion of the instructional day a student must attend to be counted present for the full day from 63% to 66%.
April Crozier, a special education teacher in Hattiesburg, said implementation will vary across the state.
“It’s going to just depend on from district to district,” Crozier said.
She said she received information about the changes as a parent but believes some families may not yet understand the requirements.
“There’s still a lot of parents out there that really don’t know or understand that there even is a new policy because they probably haven’t even looked at it,” Crozier said.
The law also calls for one school attendance officer for every 4,000 compulsory-school-age children. Marshall said MDE is working to add personnel needed to implement the changes.
As districts work toward the Nov. 1 deadline, Barnes-Woods said health care providers could help school officials develop policies that account for students’ medical needs.
“We can maybe meet and talk about the schools’ expectations and then what my goals are for my patients and educate themselves,” Barnes-Woods said.ees can also approve additional excused absences for extenuating circumstances, including prolonged illness supported by medical documentation.

name: WyoFile
title: ‘We got lucky’: Ken Roberts reflects on Mollie’s Pack and his 6 years as a Wyoming Game and Fish commissioner
description:
The district court clerk from Kemmerer, who beat a Freedom Caucus-aligned lawmaker for a House seat, nears the end of his Game and Fish term.
The post ‘We got lucky’: Ken Roberts reflects on Mollie’s Pack and his 6 years as a Wyoming Game and Fish commissioner appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
EVANSTON—Ken Roberts’ willingness to take phone calls from random numbers doesn’t always yield pleasant exchanges. That’s certainly been the case as of late for the longtime Wyoming Game and Fish commissioner, who’s nearing the end of his term. 
“I had a guy from Connecticut call me, and he wasn’t very nice,” Roberts said. “I was like half-sleeping, and he let me have it pretty good.” 
The cause of the Easterner’s consternation? Mollie’s Pack, a wolf pack named after a U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service director whose life was cut short in 1996 by cancer. That historic wolf pack moved outside of Yellowstone National Park into a legal hunting area, and the naive animals’ vulnerability generated plenty of not-so cordial outreach from animal advocates urging wildlife managers to alter Wyoming’s hunting seasons and protect the pack.   
In the end, most Mollie’s Pack wolves headed back into the park and they escaped the 2026 hunt unscathed.  
“We got lucky,” Roberts said. “We definitely got lucky.”
U.S. Interior Secretary Bruce Babbitt, left, and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Directory Mollie Beattie, third from right, carry a wolf crate into Yellowstone National Park in 1995 alongside Yellowstone National Park biologist Mike Phillips. (Courtesy National Park Service)
His past experience underlaid the remark. 
A world of outrage — and lots more calls from surly folks — would have likely awaited Roberts and his counterparts if the hunt went differently, ending Mollie’s Pack’s 31-year-long reign. 
Roberts, 64, has seen it before. He was helping steer Game and Fish when Sublette County resident Cody Roberts brought a badly injured wolf into a bar for laughs, and the severity of his punishment was the equivalent of a traffic ticket. (County law enforcement disagreed about applicable laws being violated and two years later, he pled guilty to felony animal cruelty.)
The ugly incident and the state agency’s initial response funneled an overwhelming torrent of scorn upon Wyoming. State wildlife officials caught the brunt of it. 
“That was my low on the commission,” Roberts said. 
There’ve been plenty of happier times and proud accomplishments during his tenure, too. Gov. Mark Gordon appointed Roberts as a Game and Fish commissioner in 2021 under unusual circumstances: He replaced commissioner Mike Schmid, who was involuntarily removed from his post. 

Game and Fish Commissioner Ken Roberts discusses pronghorn during a September 2025 meeting in Lander. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)

Nearly six years later, the district court clerk from Kemmerer has endured and is readying for some big life changes. This summer he suffered a brain aneurysm. Weeks after that, Roberts beat out House Majority Floor Leader Scott Heiner by a 10% margin in a race to represent Wyoming House District 18. His election victory over Heiner, an early member of the Wyoming Freedom Caucus, was part of the statewide drubbing that brought the once-powerful Republican faction to its knees. 
On Tuesday, Roberts sat down with WyoFile to discuss his experience on the Game and Fish commission and anticipated duties as a state lawmaker. This interview has been edited, organized and condensed for clarity. 
WyoFile: When you were appointed, the governor had just ousted somebody who often spoke his mind and wouldn’t always go along with the rest of the Game and Fish Commission. Did that make you especially careful as you jumped into the role? 
Roberts: No. I realized what had been going on with the commission. There had been a lot of turmoil. I know that the governor didn’t really want to make the change and I know the commission didn’t really make the change, but it got to the point where they had to do something. The governor called and said, ‘We got some turmoil going on, I’ve got to release a commissioner. Would you be willing to serve?’ I said, ‘Absolutely, in a New York second.’ I’ve always really admired the commission. 

WF: One observation from my time covering Game and Fish during your tenure is that several times, the commission trumped the department’s recommendations. The mountain lion hunting regulations come to mind and also the proposed exclusion of portions of the Sublette Pronghorn migration corridor. What was the backstory to those decisions? 
R: I felt a strong need that it was something we had to do. I told myself, ‘I’m the voice of the wildlife — if I don’t do it, nobody will.’ That’s why I advocated for the 10 corridor segments. I truly still believe to this day that we should have designated everything. [Ed’s note: Gov. Mark Gordon overrode the commission, again excluding protections for pronghorn in the Red Desert and east of Farson.] I respect the governor’s standpoint, but I would have designated the whole lot of them. I still think they need it. Red Desert pronghorn, they’re the most iconic thing we have in this state, almost. With mountain lions, we really didn’t think the science was there. We didn’t have a good feeling. 
WF: This just came up during your meeting from a retiree, but what’s happened with the director of Game and Fish and the morale of employees? It seems to me it took a dive and field staff became disillusioned with leadership. Obviously, a change was made. What’s your view? Do you agree it’s been a tough era for morale? 
R: I think we had such strong leadership with [Brian] Nesvik. I think it was tough for Angi [Bruce]. She had a tough time following Nesvik. She’s brilliant when it comes to federal projects, things like that. I never had any issues with her. The thing that was important to me, she jumped all over — the Highway 189 crossings, coming into Kemmerer. 
But her ideas didn’t sit well with rank-and-file types — wardens or biologists who have been there for 15, 20 years. She was more top-down than boots on the ground. It was unfortunate that we got into that situation. She had a vision. It didn’t coincide with the vision that the department and the governor and everybody else had.
Construction crews finish work on the overpass that’s part of a $30 million-plus wildlife crossing project going in on a 30-mile stretch of U.S. Highway 189 south of Kemmerer. (Mike Koshmrl/WyoFile)
WF: I wanted to ask you about the migration policy. Of course, it was just used on the Sublette Pronghorn corridor and celebrated and rightly so. But designation also took many years. It has no effect on private land. There are dozens and dozens of migrations waiting unprotected. Do you worry we’re not doing enough? 
R: We’re the only state in the Lower 48 that can pull any of this off. Nobody else can even come close. [Our policy] doesn’t have much teeth, but at least it puts us at the table to talk. I do want to see us press the gas. If I had my way, I’d designate about six more. We’re the last place. When it’s gone from us, it’s gone from everywhere. Industry, they don’t particularly see eye to eye with [the migration policy]. But I’m 100% for protecting the wildlife at all costs. Business finds a way. Our wildlife doesn’t have that opportunity to find a way, so we have to go strong for the wildlife.
WF: You say Wyoming is the best place left for some of these resources. That’s very true for sagebrush — the habitat and the critters that depend on it, like sage grouse and mule deer. They’re struggling.  Do you worry that we’re not doing enough to hold the line for these species?
R: To me, it’s all about connectivity. If you give these animals and birds connectivity and habitat, they’ll take care of themselves. But they can’t adjust to development. They’re just not capable of doing that. Cheatgrass, all of the above [threats], they just don’t keep up with it. Deer are the ones that just can’t figure it out. Elk do a lot better. Elk are figuring it out, and we’ve got an explosion of elk everywhere. The whitetails are coming in, and they run out the mule deer. The mule deer don’t know where to go.
WF: You’ve been a commissioner during a couple of incidents that became sensations and went viral. You’re on the receiving end of a deluge, and I’d guess probably some threats and nasty remarks. What has that experience been like? Just now, with the Mollie’s Pack situation, is there anything you wish the agency would have done differently? 
R: Out of the hundreds and hundreds of Mollie’s Pack emails I’ve been getting, they all say the same thing: ‘Wolves don’t know an imaginary line.’ Well, every unit and every place we hunt has imaginary lines. The agency looks at animals as a population, but once you allow somebody to name an animal you’re in trouble. Whether it’s 1090 from the Mollie’s or Felicia [the grizzly bear], once you put a Disney name to it that gets everybody fired up. Then you get some wild person saying, ‘I’ll shoot every damn one.’ We have to come in and play clean up. You could argue that we could have done something to protect that pack. But then the next thing you know, we’ll have another pack somewhere and people are going to be asking for the same thing. 
WF: And when you look back at the Cody Roberts incident, do you have any regrets about how Game and Fish conducted itself?
R: No. The Game and Fish tried everything. A week before it all broke, Nesvik called and said, ‘Hey, we’ve got a problem, and we’ve done everything we think we could do.’ If we were going to do anything differently, maybe make it a must-appear. But they looked into it and said this is all you’re going to get him for. 
Cody Roberts exits his change of plea hearing at the Sublette County Courthouse on March 5, 2026 in Pinedale. Roberts pleaded guilty to felony animal cruelty. (Amber Baesler/WyoFile)
WF: Let’s just be clear here. He was later charged with and pled guilty to a felony under the existing laws. 
R: He was. But it wasn’t Game and Fish. County attorneys, it was cruelty to animals he got charged with. I questioned whether that was an actual felony. I don’t think it met the elements needed to be a felony. But I’m glad he got it. What an idiot. That was an idiotic thing to do. Plain and simple, he was being an idiot.
WF: You’ve been accessible to the public as a commissioner. And I know you’ve built bridges with people who are not hunters and anglers. What have you learned from those relationships?
R: Speaking for myself, I truly believe that it takes everybody to figure out these damn problems with wildlife. I learned that in Jackson. Everybody wants to help wildlife, but we do it in different ways. We have a different way of looking at things. We’ve got to remember that we’re not right all the time, and that other people’s opinions and their life experiences are just as just as notable as our own. That’s why I get along with them. I always listen to what they have to say. If I hurt anybody’s feelings, or industry’s mad at me, or the anti-hunting groups are mad at me, I don’t care. I really try to look at it through the perspective of trying to make things as good as possible for wildlife. 
WF: Let’s segue to what comes next. What inspired you to run for a seat in the Wyoming House? 
R: I always loved the Legislature. My original idea was that I was going to run in two years — I was going to retire, and be done with Game and Fish. But then the timing was right. Politics is timing. The Freedom Caucus had shown their cards. My opponent was one of the founding members of the Freedom Caucus. When I ran, I had to get that word out. 
Members and allies of the Wyoming Freedom Caucus, including, from left: Reps. Ann Lucas, Nina Webber, Scott Heiner, Bill Allemand, Joel Guggenmos and John Bear, as well as Ken Pendergraft, Pepper Ottman and Joe Webb (in back row, not visible), Rachel Williams and Darin McCann hold a press conference on the opening day of the 68th Wyoming Legislature’s budget session in Cheyenne. All pictured except for Bill Allemand and Pepper Ottman, who was uncontested in the primary election, lost their seats to challengers. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)
WF: You weren’t happy with the Freedom Caucus? 
R: I was disgusted. In my opinion, they were taking orders from out of state. They wouldn’t communicate with anybody on the floor. And they would all vote the same. As the new Legislature comes in, I don’t think we’ll do that.
WF: What has you most psyched for the upcoming legislative session? Are there any issues inspired by your time on the commission that you want to affect in the legislature? 
R: We need to try to get the schools turned around. Let the teachers teach. Let the administrators be administrators. We have school boards — they’re ‘closest to the people’ who should be telling schools how much screen time, things like that.
I want to somehow get the railroads to have to report on how much wildlife they hit. If they hit a herd of antelope, they have to report it to the Game and Fish. Even if a semi [truck] hits an animal, they should have to report it to the port — even if it didn’t hurt their vehicle.
I’d like to see [hunting and fishing] license fees go up. I mean, you’re paying $200 to fuel up your truck, your four wheelers and your side by sides. What’s another $5, $10 for the licenses? That’s just my pipe dream.
WF: Do you think it’s high time for the Legislature to cede control to Game and Fish, so the agency can charge what it wants for a license?
R: Game and Fish should be able to manage wildlife. That’s part of managing wildlife. I’ve got to be careful. But I think Game and Fish should be allowed to manage wildlife, just like schools can manage schools, hospitals can manage hospitals.
